name: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
lead: Where this patient sits in the intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma pathway, and what the evidence behind the next step actually shows.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 1 · Diagnosis confirmed and staged
crit: Histology consistent with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, or a high-suspicion mass accepted for direct resection after multidisciplinary HPB review
Multiphase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus liver MRI with cholangiographic (MRCP) sequences, completed before any stent is placed
Another primary excluded — colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging and a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel as indicated
Perihilar and distal cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma recognised as outside this pathway
Recorded: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology
gates.ask: Do I actually know this is intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and do I have the imaging to plan an operation?

standard.t: There is no imaging-only diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, where LR-5 imaging in an at-risk population is diagnostic, a mass suspected of being iCCA requires histologic confirmation before a treatment pathway is assigned.
standard.pref: Every patient whose next step is systemic therapy, trial entry or tissue-defined transplant assessment — in those destinations the tissue criteria are not optional, and transplant assessment additionally needs the biopsy to grade differentiation and to exclude a mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma.
standard.avoid: Do not demand a core from a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass as a universal rule. NCCN states a suspicious mass on imaging in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant, and multidisciplinary HPB review may permit direct resection; the roadmap replaces universal pre-treatment biopsy with destination-specific confirmation.
standard.note: AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation and LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass, so whether a core stays mandatory before resection is a ratification item (alignment worksheet, area 1). CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis; CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction or cholangitis, so record it alongside the bilirubin and repeat it once the obstruction is relieved.

standard.t: Image before you instrument: complete the biliary-protocol imaging, and measure the future liver remnant on the same study where a major hepatectomy is contemplated.
standard.pref: Any patient with a tumour obstructing the biliary tree who might be resected — reactive change from a stent obscures ductal extent, which is exactly what decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed. MRI is the study that characterises the biliary and vascular relationships that determine resectability, and EASL-ILCA prefers it over CT for intrahepatic staging.
standard.avoid: Do not wait for imaging in cholangitis — that is drained without waiting for the discussion, and urgent sepsis treatment takes priority over the elective sequence.
standard.note: Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure; resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large. That drainage rule is grade D on its own — no comparative outcome data in intrahepatic disease were identified for it — while the grade B on this string covers the imaging sequence, which BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA both recommend.

standard.t: Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
standard.pref: Any adenocarcinoma in the liver without an established primary, and particularly before a patient is started on a biliary-tract regimen or entered into a biliary trial.
standard.avoid: Do not let the immunohistochemical panel consume the whole core: BSG 2023 asks that tissue be reserved for molecular profiling when immunohistochemistry is planned, and whether to add that instruction is a ratification item (alignment worksheet, area 12).
standard.note: Treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recognised and consequential error. Hepatitis B and C status and any cirrhosis are established at entry: they change operative risk and, where a mixed tumour is possible, the differential.

alt.t: Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure.
alt.pref: The patient entering the pathway as an indeterminate stricture, where pathology alone is weakest: in a 6-year prospective study of 2,116 patients across 28 institutions, pathologic assessment of ERCP brushings and biopsies had 44% sensitivity overall and 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures, while a DNA/RNA sequencing panel on separately collected specimens in a dedicated nucleic-acid buffer reached 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity and the combination 88% at 97%. Specificity was 99% for pathology, so sequencing bought sensitivity and gave up almost nothing.
alt.avoid: Do not read a negative molecular result as excluding malignancy — in the original single-centre cohort there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value was only 63%, with sampling failure the usual explanation; in 12 of those cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures in the 2026 study were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no resectability or survival benefit has been shown. Payer authorisation and the dedicated collection buffer have to be arranged before the procedure, not after.
alt.note: Correct the yield figure: therapeutically relevant alterations were reported in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) in the original single-centre cohort, and in the 2026 multi-institutional study in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%) — but only on the 161-gene version of the panel. The 28-gene version used in the original cohort did not detect FGFR2 fusions at all, which with chromatin-remodelling genes accounts for up to 20% of intrahepatic tumours, so a biliary specimen substitutes for the gate 2 profile only if the panel actually run reports fusions. Downgraded from B: specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, a stricture could be classified neoplastic on 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay.

alt.t: Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging.
alt.pref: Where occult nodal or distant disease would change the operation, and in any patient being staged for a transplant protocol.
alt.avoid: Do not substitute PET for MRI with MRCP in local planning; MRCP is preferred for biliary anatomy and ERCP or PTC are used more for therapeutic intervention.
alt.note: BSG 2023 recommends FDG-PET-CT for nodal and distant disease as part of staging and EASL-ILCA recommends it routinely in apparently resectable patients, both more broadly than our selective wording — alignment worksheet, area 2. Read the strength of the broader recommendation honestly: the EASL-ILCA routine-PET statement passed its Delphi panel with only 78% agreement, the weakest consensus in that guideline's staging section, and AASLD 2023 states PET should not be used to assess the primary tumour.

avoid.t: Do not place a biliary stent in a potentially resectable patient before the biliary-protocol imaging is complete and the drainage plan is agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon.
avoid.pref: The only exception is cholangitis, which is drained immediately.
avoid.avoid: Stent-related inflammation obscures ductal extent, and drainage of the wrong side or an unnecessary procedure adds cholangitis risk and can delay both surgery and systemic therapy.

avoid.t: Do not assign this pathway to perihilar or distal cholangiocarcinoma — the drainage problem, the operation and the transplant question all differ.
avoid.pref: Use the separate perihilar roadmap; gallbladder cancer, mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma and paediatric disease are out of scope here.
avoid.avoid: In particular, the standardised perihilar MELD exception and its neoadjuvant/stricture protocol do not transfer to intrahepatic disease.

gates.name: 2 · Molecular profile ordered at diagnosis
crit: Unresectable or metastatic disease at diagnosis — order now, not at the point of second-line progression
Borderline or locally advanced disease where systemic therapy is the first step
Recurrence after resection that will be treated systemically
Adequate tissue preserved from the diagnostic core, or plasma where tissue is inadequate or a biopsy would delay treatment
gates.ask: Will the molecular result be in my hand at the moment the second-line decision is made?

standard.t: Order broad molecular profiling at the diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease, not at the point of second-line progression.
standard.pref: Everyone who will receive systemic therapy. The rationale is operational rather than biological: turnaround is typically two to four weeks, and a patient who progresses on first-line chemo-immunotherapy needs the result in hand at that moment.
standard.avoid: Ordering it at progression means the second-line decision is made without it, and the default becomes FOLFOX by omission rather than by choice. The obstacle here is payer authorisation and ordering discipline, not the clinical argument.
standard.note: Our grade B is lower than ESMO 2024's [I, A] and BSG 2023's strong recommendation on high-quality evidence. ILTS-ILCA 2024 recommends comprehensive sequencing in unresectable or metastatic iCCA but finds no evidence for using it to select transplant candidates. Capture NRG1 and other actionable findings on the same panel; do not label each matched agent category 1 merely because testing is recommended.

opts.name: FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype. Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum. At final FIGHT-202 analysis, independently reviewed response was 37.0% with median progression-free survival 7.0 months and median overall survival 17.5 months in 108 patients; FOENIX-CCA2 gave response 42%, median progression-free survival 9.0 months and median overall survival 21.7 months in 103 patients.
opts.pref: Second line or later in a patient fit for an oral targeted agent, where the alteration reported is a fusion or rearrangement — 90% of FIGHT-202 and the whole of FOENIX-CCA2 was intrahepatic disease, so this is the alteration with the most directly applicable data.
opts.avoid: Do not infer superiority over second-line chemotherapy: both trials are single-arm, neither has been compared with it, and the pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy (response 9.5%, progression-free survival 2.6 months) that makes the agent look better. Both drugs were approved on these single-arm data. Do not expect the alteration in an untested patient — 783 patients were screened to enrol 103 in FOENIX-CCA2, and 1,206 were prescreened to find 107 fusion-positive patients for FIGHT-202.
opts.note: At the FIGHT-202 final analysis there were no objective responses in the cohorts with other FGF/FGFR alterations (0 of 20) or with none (0 of 17), so the effect is confined to the fusion and rearrangement class; with 20 and 17 patients that is a weak negative rather than proof. Hyperphosphataemia affected 58.5% on pemigatinib and 85% on futibatinib (grade 3 in 30%), and acquired kinase-domain resistance mutations emerged in those who shrank then progressed. Benefit is modest in absolute terms and the first-line question is still open in FIGHT-302.

opts.name: IDH1 mutation
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype, positioned on progression-free survival grounds only. ClarIDHy met its primary endpoint — median progression-free survival 2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37 — but the final intention-to-treat overall survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), p=0.09, not significant, with 70% of placebo patients crossing over.
opts.pref: A chemotherapy-refractory patient with an IDH1 mutation who understands that the benefit is disease stabilisation: objective response was 2% and the signal came from stable disease, 51% versus 28%. Physical functioning was better preserved than on placebo.
opts.avoid: Do not use it to convert unresectable disease — response is almost absent, so it is useless as an on-treatment surgical decision point. Do not quote the crossover-adjusted survival figure (hazard ratio 0.49) as the trial result; it comes from a model that assumes the effect is identical whenever given.
opts.note: The comparator was placebo, not the active second-line standard, so the gain over mFOLFOX is unknown. Note the population when reading this into a liver pathway: only 9 of 185 patients (5%) had cirrhosis, 93% were metastatic and 90% of the ivosidenib arm had intrahepatic disease, so this is a non-cirrhotic metastatic cohort and nothing like a transplant or conversion candidate. Quality-of-life conclusions rest on change scores available for 62 of 113 ivosidenib and 20 of 52 placebo patients.

opts.name: BRAF V600E
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype. Dabrafenib plus trametinib: single-arm, 43 patients, response 51% by investigator and 47% by independent review, median progression-free survival 9 months and median overall survival 14 months — interim analysis.
opts.pref: A previously treated patient with a centrally confirmable V600E mutation; 39 of the 43 patients (91%) had intrahepatic disease, so the population matches.
opts.avoid: Do not expect the trial's 9% screening yield in practice — several sites entered already-known positives and the real rate is nearer 5–7%. Patients with bilirubin above three times normal or untreatable biliary obstruction were excluded, so this says nothing about the jaundiced patient.

opts.name: HER2 amplification or overexpression
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype. Zanidatamab: single-arm; at final analysis (median follow-up 33.4 months, 80 ERBB2-amplified patients) confirmed response was 41% (33 of 80, 95% CI 30–53) and median overall survival 15.5 months.
opts.pref: An IHC 3+ tumour, where the activity is concentrated: response 52% (32 of 62) versus 6% (1 of 18) at IHC 2+, disease control 79% versus 33%, and median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — a post hoc split the authors themselves label as such.
opts.avoid: Do not offer it on an IHC 2+ result as though the trial supported it, and do not read the 15.5-month survival as attributable to the drug: there was no control group and 44% of patients received further anticancer therapy afterwards.
opts.note: Results are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite, so the effect specifically in intrahepatic disease is unknown; HER2 is a minority of iCCA. ESMO 2024 also recommends considering trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2 overexpression or amplification, which our table does not name — alignment worksheet, area 14.

opts.name: MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype. Checkpoint blockade, consistent with tumour-agnostic practice.
opts.pref: The small hypermutated subset — and it is small: only 5 of 333 evaluable patients in TOPAZ-1 and 10 in KEYNOTE-966 were MSI-high.
opts.avoid: Do not recycle checkpoint blockade without accounting for prior exposure to first-line durvalumab or pembrolizumab.

opts.name: NTRK fusion, RET fusion, other actionable alterations
opts.when: Reasonable consideration. Capture on the same broad panel so a later line is not delayed by re-testing.
opts.pref: Any patient being profiled — the panel costs nothing extra and removes a re-testing delay.
opts.avoid: Do not treat capture as a licence to prescribe: ESMO 2024 recommends NTRK inhibitors and selpercatinib for RET fusions on level III evidence, while our table only requires that these alterations be captured. Whether to name the agents is a ratification item.

standard.order: This order reproduces the roadmap's table. It is not a ranking: each option applies only to the patient whose tumour carries that alteration, and there is no randomised evidence establishing a sequence among the targeted options. Only ivosidenib comes from a randomised trial, and that trial was positive on progression-free survival and not on intention-to-treat overall survival; the others are single-arm response data, not comparative survival data.
standard.flagnote: Match treatment to the alteration class reported, not to the gene name. The evidence above is for FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, IDH1 mutation, BRAF V600E, HER2 amplification or overexpression, and MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficiency; other alterations in the same genes are not interchangeable and should be reviewed with a clinician experienced in molecular oncology before a matched agent is chosen — Standard, grade D. Whether the HER2 row names trastuzumab deruxtecan and the NTRK/RET row names agents, as ESMO 2024 does, is a ratification item (alignment worksheet, area 14).

alt.t: Use circulating tumour DNA when tissue is inadequate or the biopsy would delay treatment.
alt.pref: The patient whose core is exhausted or whose repeat biopsy would push the start of treatment out by weeks.
alt.avoid: Do not accept a negative plasma result as excluding a target — BSG 2023 notes DNA-based panels and most liquid biopsies are weaker at detecting fusions, so a negative plasma result should prompt tissue testing where it would change management.
alt.note: Read the plasma figure for what it is: the FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement was detectable in plasma in 83 of 95 FOENIX-CCA2 patients tested (87%), but those patients were already known to be tissue-positive, so 87% is concordance in a positive population and not the chance of finding a target de novo in an unselected patient. No study in this disease reports the latter.

avoid.t: Do not defer profiling to the point of second-line progression.
avoid.pref: Order it at diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease; audit the proportion profiled before the second-line decision.
avoid.avoid: The failure mode is not a wrong choice but no choice: the second-line decision gets made without the result, and FOLFOX becomes the default by omission.

gates.name: 3 · Resectable now
crit: R0 achievable: solitary or clustered disease clearable with an adequate functional remnant
Inflow, outflow and biliary drainage preservable or reconstructable
No nodal disease beyond the regional basin — no retroperitoneal or coeliac stations
No extrahepatic disease
Adequate reserve and performance status for the operation the anatomy requires
gates.ask: Can I take all of this out with a negative margin and leave enough working liver?

opts.name: Resection with regional lymphadenectomy
opts.when: The established curative standard. Hepatic resection with negative margins is the goal; major resections are often necessary but wedge and segmental resections are appropriate where a negative margin can be achieved, and a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis is carried out.
opts.pref: Liver-confined disease where R0 is achievable with an adequate remnant and preserved or reconstructable biliary drainage, in a patient fit for the operation. Lymphadenectomy is part of the operation and informs the adjuvant decision in gate 8 — nodal status is the main staging variable afterwards and clinical nodal staging is insensitive.
opts.avoid: Multifocal disease across both lobes, satellite pattern implying field disease, encasement precluding reconstruction, bilateral second-order biliary involvement, nodal disease beyond the regional basin, any extrahepatic disease, or reserve that makes the necessary resection unsafe.
opts.note: Nodal status and tumour number dominate outcome: LCSGJ 2022 reports 5-year survival of 46.8%, 33.6% and 11.1% for one, two and three tumours, 63.4% for tumours under 2 cm, and 7–19% with nodal metastasis. The lymphadenectomy itself is the weak point in the evidence, not the resection: LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation on node dissection at all and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications, ESMO 2023 recommends routine hepatoduodenal-ligament dissection on level IV evidence, and neither BSG 2023 nor AASLD 2023 states an extent or a minimum node yield. Keeping it in every operation is a staging decision the programme has made, not a survival finding.

opts.name: Definitive thermal ablation
opts.when: Potentially curative in a narrow nonsurgical group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. NCCN accepts thermal ablation for a small single primary or recurrent iCCA under 3 cm, particularly where surgery carries high risk; EASL-ILCA is narrower at single lesions under 2 cm, unresectable or inoperable, on low-level evidence.
opts.pref: The small single lesion in a patient whose reserve or comorbidity makes resection unsuitable, where all disease can be treated with a margin of 5 mm or more and there is no uncontrolled nodal or distant disease. In a ten-centre propensity-matched cohort, microwave ablation gave 5-year overall survival of 44.8% versus 40.4% for resection (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71–1.29, p=0.761), and when both ablative and surgical margins exceeded 5 mm disease-free survival was also similar (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.52–1.32, p=0.41).
opts.avoid: No safe margin obtainable, central bile duct injury risk, or disease left unaddressed. Do not extrapolate to large or multifocal tumours: in meta-analysis, tumours over 3 cm (HR 2.12) and multiple tumours (HR 1.67) carried shorter survival, and pooled 5-year survival after ablation was 28.5%.
opts.note: Disease-free survival in the matched cohort favoured resection overall (median 1.7 versus 3.6 years, HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.48–0.83, p=0.0010), with margin mediating 34.5% of that gap. Two cautions the cohort itself imposes. First, its entry criterion was Milan-equivalent — a single tumour up to 5 cm or up to three each 3 cm or less — so it does not validate our under-3 cm wording; within it, a 3–5 cm tumour was an independent risk factor for disease-free survival after ablation but not after resection, and resection also outperformed ablation in patients under 60, with hepatolithiasis, with left-lobe tumours and with GGT above 50 U/L. Second, the equivalence headline comes from a post hoc split at 2017 in which the later comparison was underpowered (p=0.129), and a nonsignificant difference is not equivalence. Ablation also yields no specimen and no nodal dissection, so the patient has no pathological node status to drive the gate 8 decision, and node-negativity rests on imaging whose sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61%. Agreeing the boundary — NCCN under 3 cm versus EASL-ILCA under 2 cm — is a ratification item.

opts.name: Ablative radiotherapy for inoperable localized disease
opts.when: Selected definitive or consolidative treatment where the disease is localized but the patient is inoperable; cure evidence is limited. It may be selected directly on geometry and reserve — unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite.
opts.pref: Localized, liver-confined disease in a patient who cannot have an operation or an ablation, with adequate uninvolved liver, relieved biliary obstruction and safe gastrointestinal and biliary doses. A retrospective dose-response analysis of 79 patients found 3-year overall survival of 73% with a biologic equivalent dose above 80.5 Gy versus 38% below it (p=0.017) and 3-year local control 78% versus 45% (p=0.04); a multi-institutional phase II proton study reported 2-year local control of 94.1% in its 39 iCCA patients with grade 3 toxicity in 7.7%.
opts.avoid: Insufficient uninvolved liver, unrelieved biliary obstruction, overlapping prior dose or refractory ascites. For bulky disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default.
opts.note: Both datasets are nonrandomised and selected. Only 19 of 79 patients received the high dose, and that group also had significantly smaller planning target volumes (median 415 versus 614 cm³, p=0.02), so more favourable anatomy is confounded with dose; dose escalation is further confounded with era and image guidance, since patients treated after 2010 survived 50 versus 24 months (p=0.007). The proton cohort had no prespecified efficacy hypothesis at all — it was enrolled alongside a hepatocellular cohort for precision of estimates — its median delivered dose was 58.0 GyE against an intended 67.5 GyE, every local failure occurred below 60 GyE, local failures kept accruing past the 2-year landmark (six in 39) and 53.8% developed distant metastases. Dose-response associations do not prove cure or equivalence to resection.

standard.order: Resection is first because it is the established curative standard, not because the alternatives have been shown to be inferior in a randomised trial — none exists in this disease. Ablation sits second on one large propensity-matched cohort plus guideline wording, ablative radiotherapy third on retrospective dose-response and single-arm phase II data with explicitly weaker cure evidence. The order reflects the guidelines' wording and the depth of each dataset, not a demonstrated survival advantage.
standard.flagnote: Three ratification items sit on this gate. First, 'regional basin' is undefined in v0.6; AASLD 2023 draws the boundary at nodal metastasis beyond the hepatoduodenal and gastrohepatic ligaments, and an undefined basin is hard to audit (area 3). Second, the roadmap is silent on portal hypertension while AASLD 2023 names decompensated cirrhosis and/or portal hypertension contraindications to resection; numeric reserve rules remain specialty-approved local implementation (area 4). Third, routine lymphadenectomy is kept for every resection, where LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications (area 5).

alt.t: Consider resection for limited multifocal disease only in highly selected cases, as an explicit exception rather than a rule.
alt.pref: Unilobar limited multifocal disease in a fit patient where an R0 clearance with an adequate remnant is genuinely achievable — EASL-ILCA suggests resection may be considered in selected patients with multifocal unilobar iCCA (weak recommendation), and LCSGJ 2022 accepts resection for some node-positive patients.
alt.avoid: NCCN states that multifocal liver disease is generally representative of metastatic disease and is a contraindication to resection. Do not turn a narrow exception into unrestricted eligibility; a satellite pattern implying field disease belongs in gate 4 or 5.

alt.t: Consider neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy where the disease is technically resectable but only an R1 resection looks achievable.
alt.pref: The technically challenging but resectable tumour where the surgeon's honest assessment is that the margin will be positive — EASL-ILCA considers this (weak recommendation, 92% consensus), and BSG 2023 recommends multidisciplinary re-discussion of curative resection in locally advanced disease that responds well.
alt.avoid: Not in clearly resectable disease, where the roadmap places neoadjuvant therapy off protocol in the Avoid column and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Record the obstacle to R0 and the reassessment date, exactly as in gate 4.

avoid.t: Do not give neoadjuvant therapy off protocol in clearly resectable disease.
avoid.pref: Operate, then have the adjuvant conversation in gate 8.
avoid.avoid: BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy for resectable disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence) and LCSGJ 2022 found no evidence of benefit; the cost of delay is a resection not performed.

avoid.t: Do not operate in the presence of nodal disease beyond the regional basin or any extrahepatic disease.
avoid.pref: Any extrahepatic disease moves the pathway to systemic and molecularly directed therapy — gate 6.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states lymph node metastases beyond the porta hepatis and distant metastatic disease contraindicate resection; AASLD 2023 prefers upfront chemotherapy and treats later rescue surgery as individualised.

gates.name: 4 · Resectable after conversion
crit: Not R0 now, and the specific obstacle to R0 is recorded
No extrahepatic disease
What would have to change for resection to become possible is recorded alongside the plan
A reassessment date at 2–3 months is declared before treatment starts
Fit for the systemic regimen that is the backbone of any conversion attempt
gates.ask: What exactly has to change for this to become resectable, and when will I look?

standard.t: Systemic therapy with a scheduled surgical reassessment at 2–3 months. The obstacle to R0 and what would have to change must both be recorded.
standard.pref: Borderline or locally advanced liver-confined disease in a patient fit for chemo-immunotherapy, where conversion is a declared goal rather than a hope. Reassessment at the pre-declared point is a formal surgical re-review, not an imaging report alone.
standard.avoid: Do not run conversion therapy open-endedly. If R0 is not achievable at the reassessment, say so and record that the goal has changed from conversion to control — that is the decision the board has to make.
standard.note: The conversion figures are weaker than they sound. The rates of 36.4% and 53% come from retrospective Japanese series quoted by LCSGJ 2022, which in the same breath records no evidence of benefit for neoadjuvant chemotherapy and makes no recommendation; the denominators are not defined and the series report median survival of 24.1 months in converted patients against 25.7 months in those primarily resectable. AASLD 2023 states the role of neoadjuvant downstaging is not well defined, and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The roadmap grades this pathway C for those reasons. Note also that neither chemo-immunotherapy trial supports it: TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and neither says anything about downstaging.

opts.name: Hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic chemotherapy
opts.when: Conversion or hepatic control in an approved expert programme, generally with systemic therapy; no established cure as monotherapy. In a single-arm, single-institution phase 2 study of 38 treated patients, HAI floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine–oxaliplatin gave partial response in 22 of 38 (58%) and 6-month progression-free survival of 84.1% against an 80% target, with median progression-free survival 11.8 months and median overall survival 25.0 months, and four patients went on to resection.
opts.pref: Liver-confined unresectable disease with favourable arterial anatomy in a centre with a functioning pump programme, where conversion or durable hepatic control is the stated goal. It can be considered early rather than only after a systemic line fails.
opts.avoid: No dedicated pump programme, any extrahepatic disease, or unrelieved biliary obstruction. Do not treat it as interchangeable with a modern chemo-immunotherapy regimen, and do not count response as the curative event — conversion to a complete operation is.
opts.note: Grade 4 toxicity forcing withdrawal occurred in 4 of 38 (11%) of the phase 2 cohort (portal hypertension, two gastroduodenal artery aneurysms, pump-pocket infection), grade 3 ALT in 42% and AST in 34%, and 11% needed biliary stents, two for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis. Delivery decayed: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months but only 47% over the next 6. The cohort was heavily selected — 38 of 84 screened, median tumour 8.3 cm — and the comparison is with historical systemic series; the linked JAMA Oncology editorial judged the case for locoregional therapy in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma still unsettled without a randomised trial. A retrospective single-centre comparison gave median overall survival of 30.8 months with HAI plus systemic therapy versus 18.4 months with systemic therapy alone in liver-confined disease, but all HAI patients were surgically staged and only 42% of the comparator was, so stage migration favours HAI; the comparator was 26 patients of whom only 30% had gemcitabine–cisplatin, and 44 of the 93 HAI patients came from two previously reported phase 2 trials. In that whole series only 8 of 236 patients (3%) converted to a curative-intent resection.

opts.name: Y90 radioembolisation with first-line chemotherapy
opts.when: Control or conversion with selected ablative use under expert review; curative evidence is emerging, not established. MISPHEC, a single-arm phase II study of 41 patients, combined Y90 with gemcitabine–cisplatin: response at 3 months was 39% by investigator assessment and 41% centrally, 9 patients (22%) were downstaged to surgery and 8 (20%) achieved an R0 resection, with median overall survival 22 months.
opts.pref: Liver-dominant unresectable disease in a non-cirrhotic patient with personalised dosimetry available, where conversion is the explicit plan — among the 27 patients with disease confined to one hemiliver, 8 (30%) were resected.
opts.avoid: Cirrhosis above all: hepatic failure occurred in 9 of 12 cirrhotic patients (75%), irreversible in 5, versus 5 of 29 (17%) without cirrhosis, all reversible, and every irreversible case had whole-liver treatment. The trial's authors advise against radioembolisation plus chemotherapy in cirrhosis. Also avoid with inadequate future remnant or an unsafe shunt fraction.
opts.note: Those results do not prove Y90 alone is curative, and grade 3–4 toxicity affected 29 of 41 patients (71%). The conversion figures describe a doubly selected cohort: 4 of 45 patients were excluded at the planning angiogram and 9 of 41 had major protocol deviations, leaving 32 per protocol. The trial was run only at centres experienced with glass microspheres and was part-funded by the microsphere manufacturer, with several authors as its consultants; the authors state tumour-absorbed dose rather than a generic liver dose probably drives outcome, so the regimen does not transfer as written. Two patients whose disease stayed unresectable but controlled were offered transplant and both recurred, at 16 and 17 months. The NCCN discussion of a tumour dose above 205 Gy is distinct from hepatocellular segment-dose thresholds. Payer authorisation and dosimetry capability are local dependencies, and the confirmatory randomised SIRCCA trial has not reported.

opts.name: Liver-directed radiotherapy where conversion is the goal
opts.when: Ablative or hypofractionated radiotherapy as the liver-directed component of a conversion strategy, selected on geometry and reserve.
opts.pref: Disease whose obstacle to resection is a single geometric relationship that dose can address, in a patient with adequate uninvolved liver and relieved biliary obstruction.
opts.avoid: Insufficient uninvolved liver, unrelieved biliary obstruction, overlapping prior dose or refractory ascites. The conversion evidence here is weaker than for HAI or Y90: the dose-response and proton datasets report local control and survival, not resection rates.

alt.order: No head-to-head comparison exists between these, and none has been tested against a modern chemo-immunotherapy backbone. The order follows the depth of the conversion data specifically — HAI and Y90 both report patients actually taken to resection (4 of 38 and 9 of 41), radiotherapy does not — and the roadmap's own condition that conversion be the explicit goal and the programme exist. It carries no survival claim.
alt.flagnote: Unresolved decisions 1 and 2: whether the programme runs a hepatic arterial infusion service for iCCA at all, and which liver-directed modality is first choice for unresectable liver-confined disease. Supporting data for HAI are a single-arm, largely single-institution phase 2 experience; the deciding variables are pump expertise, nursing infrastructure and case volume, not the evidence.

avoid.t: Do not run open-ended conversion therapy with no defined reassessment.
avoid.pref: Declare the reassessment point before treatment starts and hold to it; after progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider complete treatment rather than automatically repeating the same procedure.
avoid.avoid: A patient who drifts through four months of therapy without a surgical re-review has lost the conversion opportunity without anyone deciding to abandon it.

avoid.t: Do not present conversion to resection as an expected outcome.
avoid.pref: Say what the numbers are: 22% downstaged and 20% resected with R0 in the Y90 study, 4 of 38 resected in the HAI study. Conversion treatment is not itself the curative operation.
avoid.avoid: Promising conversion sets up both the patient and the programme for a decision that cannot be unmade — and a complete radiographic response is not the same outcome as an R0 resection.

gates.name: 5 · Permanently unresectable, liver-confined
crit: Not convertible at formal surgical re-review, not on an imaging report alone
No extrahepatic disease
Liver function and performance status adequate for systemic therapy
Biliary obstruction relieved, or a drainage plan agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon
gates.ask: The liver is the whole problem and I cannot operate — what holds this disease, and in what order?

standard.t: Systemic therapy is the backbone: gemcitabine and cisplatin with durvalumab, or with pembrolizumab.
standard.pref: Every patient fit for it. The regimens and the fitness question are in gate 9; what this gate settles is that systemic therapy is the backbone and any liver-directed treatment is added to it, not substituted for it.
standard.avoid: A patient whose performance status, renal or hepatic function, or contraindication to checkpoint inhibition rules out the full regimen still gets a systemic plan, modified with the reason recorded — not a catheter instead.
standard.note: Downgraded from A. The two trials that carry the grade did not study this gate's population. TOPAZ-1 was 86% metastatic and KEYNOTE-966 89%, both restricted to ECOG 0–1, and the TOPAZ-1 investigators state explicitly that the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use in liver-confined disease, which is where this regimen is now borrowed. Grade A remains right for gate 9, where the population matches. Clinical trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression — Standard, grade D.

opts.name: Hepatic arterial infusion
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype: liver-confined unresectable disease, favourable arterial anatomy, with durable hepatic control or conversion as the stated goal. 6-month progression-free survival 84.1% and median overall survival 25.0 months in a 38-patient phase 2 cohort; 30.8 versus 18.4 months against systemic therapy alone in a retrospective liver-confined comparison.
opts.pref: The strongest regional dataset in this disease, in a centre with a pump programme and the nursing infrastructure to run it. Resectable regional nodal disease did not separate outcomes in the phase 2 cohort (24-month survival 60% node-negative versus 50% node-positive, p=0.66).
opts.avoid: No dedicated pump programme, extrahepatic disease, unrelieved biliary obstruction. Grade 4 toxicity requiring withdrawal occurred in 11% of the phase 2 cohort and in 30% of the 10-patient confirmatory cohort.

opts.name: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation
opts.when: Hepatic control. Liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Median overall survival was 22 months with Y90 plus gemcitabine–cisplatin in a 41-patient phase II, and 20 months from diagnosis in a 62-patient two-centre chemoembolisation cohort, where the 18 patients who also had systemic chemotherapy survived 28 versus 16 months (HR 1.94, p=0.02).
opts.pref: Hepatic-dominant disease where selective delivery and reserve are adequate and the goal is stated as control, with the systemic plan running alongside. Procedural safety was the strongest chemoembolisation finding: major complications after 5 of 165 procedures (3%), 0% 30-day disease-specific mortality.
opts.avoid: Substitution for systemic therapy; use while extrahepatic disease progresses; inadequate future remnant or unsafe shunt fraction; biliary obstruction and infection risk. Avoid radioembolisation plus chemotherapy in cirrhosis, where hepatic failure occurred in 75% of cirrhotic patients and was irreversible in 5.
opts.note: The chemoembolisation evidence is heterogeneous and nonrandomised — 40% of that cohort had adenocarcinoma of unknown primary rather than proven cholangiocarcinoma, 11% had a prior hepatectomy, 27% had no evaluable imaging follow-up, and the regimen (an ethiodol and polyvinyl alcohol emulsion of cisplatin, doxorubicin and mitomycin) predates drug-eluting beads, Y90 and gemcitabine–cisplatin. Do not read the 28 versus 16 months as an effect of adding chemotherapy: only 18 of 62 patients received it, at their own oncologists' discretion, so those were by definition the fitter patients. None of this has evidence equivalent to resection or small-tumour ablation for eradication, and there is no proven preferred sequence among TACE, Y90, HAI and ablative radiotherapy.

opts.name: SBRT or proton therapy
opts.when: Selected definitive or consolidative local treatment for localized inoperable disease; cure evidence limited. 3-year local control 78% and 3-year overall survival 73% above a biologic equivalent dose of 80.5 Gy in a retrospective series of 79; 2-year local control 94.1% and median overall survival 22.5 months in the 39 iCCA patients of a phase II proton study.
opts.pref: Liver-confined, unresectable disease without nodal or extrahepatic involvement, where the geometry allows an ablative dose with safe gastrointestinal and biliary doses. It may be chosen directly on geometry and reserve; an unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite.
opts.avoid: Insufficient uninvolved liver, unrelieved biliary obstruction, overlapping prior dose, refractory ascites. For bulky disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default.
opts.note: Both series are selected and nonrandomised, the dose effect is confounded with era and image guidance, and in the proton cohort local failures continued past 2 years while 53.8% developed distant metastases.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: Potentially curative intent in a narrow group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. Pooled survival after ablation across 20 retrospective studies and 917 patients was 82.4% at 1 year, 42.1% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years, with technical efficacy 91.9% and major complications 5.7%.
opts.pref: The small solitary lesion in a patient unsuitable for resection, where every lesion can be covered with a margin. It is a selected definitive alternative, not automatically a second systemic line.
opts.avoid: No safe margin, central bile duct injury risk, or unaddressed disease; tumours over 3 cm and multiple tumours did worse (HR 2.12 and 1.67). Do not extrapolate to large or multifocal iCCA.
opts.note: The pooled figures are fragile: all 20 studies were retrospective, heterogeneity reached I² 85% at 1 year, Egger testing showed publication bias in the 3-year pooling (p=0.039), and disease control was short-lived even when ablation worked — pooled recurrence-free survival was 40.0% at 1 year and 19.2% at 3 years. The 3 cm threshold rests on a dichotomised study-level variable with no individual patient data, unadjusted for margin, nodal status or liver function, and the authors' own comparison of their 28.5% pooled 5-year survival with a 30% figure from a separate resection meta-analysis carries no adjustment for stage, candidacy or era.

alt.order: This is the weakest evidence zone in the pathway. No randomised trial compares any two of these modalities in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and none has been tested against a modern chemo-immunotherapy backbone, so selection is driven by treatment goal, target geometry, liver reserve and what the institution can actually deliver. The order below reproduces the roadmap's listing and the size of each dataset; it is not a hierarchy of evidence, because no such hierarchy exists.
alt.flagnote: Unresolved decisions 2, 6 and 7: which liver-directed modality is first choice here, what liver-function thresholds bar each modality (no comparative data define the cut-offs — they are safety conventions), and whether ablation is acceptable in iCCA and in whom. Dosimetry capability, device availability and payer authorisation are local dependencies, not universal ones.

avoid.t: Do not substitute liver-directed therapy for systemic therapy.
avoid.pref: Keep the systemic backbone and add hepatic control to it; coordinate the two rather than choosing between them.
avoid.avoid: AASLD 2023 states data are insufficient to recommend liver-directed therapy as a standard therapy for locally advanced unresectable iCCA. NCCN's wording that arterially directed therapies may be used alone can be read as permitting substitution; the roadmap keeps the Avoid label and puts that disagreement to a decision (alignment worksheet, area 9) — it is the one area where NCCN and this roadmap differ.

avoid.t: Do not transplant outside a protocol.
avoid.pref: Gate 10 sets out the narrow phenotype and the route. A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception.
avoid.avoid: Record bridge and downstaging treatment separately from definitive local treatment, protect liver reserve, and preserve future resection and transplant options.

avoid.t: Do not repeat the same procedure after progression without restaging and reconsidering the whole treatment plan.
avoid.pref: After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider complete treatment; an upfront alternative chosen because of anatomy or organ reserve is not a post-progression second line.
avoid.avoid: Do not use a universal ablation > SBRT > Y90 > TACE > HAI > histotripsy ladder — there is no such ladder in this disease.

gates.name: 6 · Metastatic — extrahepatic disease present
crit: Any extrahepatic disease on staging imaging
Nodal disease beyond the regional basin, including retroperitoneal or coeliac stations
A new extrahepatic site found at reassessment
Distant metastatic disease at recurrence after resection
gates.ask: Extrahepatic disease is present — what is the systemic plan, and what should I stop doing to the liver?

opts.name: Gemcitabine and cisplatin plus durvalumab (TOPAZ-1)
opts.when: Overall survival hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97), median 12.8 versus 11.5 months, with 24-month survival 24.9% versus 10.4% in 685 patients. In the intrahepatic subgroup (n=383) the hazard ratio was 0.76 (0.58–0.98).
opts.pref: A patient fit for platinum and for checkpoint inhibition who wants the regimen with the longer tail: almost all of the benefit accrues after 6 months (hazard ratio 0.91 up to 6 months, 0.74 thereafter), and gemcitabine is capped at eight cycles.
opts.avoid: Active or prior autoimmune or inflammatory disorders, or any contraindication to checkpoint inhibition. Do not promise the median — the absolute gain in median survival is 1.3 months, the proportional-hazards assumption was formally violated on kernel-smoothed and log-log plots so a single hazard ratio misrepresents a time-varying effect, and this was a prespecified interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths, powered to about 75%. The 24-month figures are Kaplan-Meier estimates, not counted survivors.
opts.note: Benefit did not track PD-L1 expression (hazard ratio 0.79 at tumour area positivity of 1% or more, 0.86 below 1%), and MSI status was missing for about half the cohort, with only 5 of 333 evaluable patients MSI-high, so the possibility that a small hypermutated subset carries the signal is answered by argument rather than data. Responses were investigator-assessed with no central review. Ampullary cancer was excluded and 86% of patients were metastatic, so the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use. Point estimates were better in locally advanced than metastatic disease (0.49 versus 0.83) but the trial was not sized for subgroups and no multiplicity adjustment was made, so that cannot be acted on.

opts.name: Gemcitabine and cisplatin plus pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-966)
opts.when: Median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, hazard ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.72–0.95) in 1069 patients, with 24-month survival 25% versus 18%. The intrahepatic subgroup (n=633) carried the effect: hazard ratio 0.76 (0.64–0.91), against 0.99 extrahepatic and 0.96 gallbladder.
opts.pref: A patient fit for checkpoint inhibition where gemcitabine continued to progression without a cycle cap suits the plan, and where the largest intrahepatic dataset is the reassurance wanted.
opts.avoid: Contraindication to checkpoint inhibition, or prior systemic therapy for advanced disease. The absolute gain is 1.8 months of median survival, and both supporting endpoints failed their prespecified boundaries — progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.86 (p=0.023 against 0.0125) and objective response 29% versus 29% (p=0.47) — so the benefit rests on overall survival with no response signal behind it. Treatment-related deaths were 8 (2%) versus 3 (1%), immune-mediated events 22% versus 13%, and quality of life did not improve (EORTC QLQ-C30 global health change −2.5 in both arms).
opts.note: There is no usable predictive biomarker: the effect was the same below and above a PD-L1 combined positive score of 1 and only 10 MSI-high patients enrolled, so every patient is exposed to immune toxicity without a way to select. Crossover was not permitted and 89% were metastatic, so the trial says nothing about perioperative or conversion strategy.

standard.order: The roadmap does not rank them. Both improved survival against chemotherapy alone and there is no head-to-head comparison, so the choice is made on toxicity profile, schedule and access — exactly ESMO 2024's position, which states no biomarker and no difference in efficacy or toxicity favours one checkpoint inhibitor over the other. Nothing in this order implies a survival advantage for either.
standard.flagnote: Our position retains an unranked checkpoint-combination choice and leaves modification to the treating oncologist; BSG 2023 regards oxaliplatin substitution in renal impairment and gemcitabine alone in poor performance status as reasonable, and whether to name those defaults is a ratification item (alignment worksheet, area 13). Reserve, infection control and transplant intent affect eligibility.

opts.name: A matched targeted agent, if a driver is present
opts.when: Second line, where the molecular result from gate 2 shows an alteration of the class the evidence covers. These are single-arm response data — pemigatinib 37.0% response and 17.5 months median survival, futibatinib 42% and 21.7 months, zanidatamab 41% and 15.5 months, dabrafenib–trametinib 51% by investigator and 47% centrally — not comparative survival data.
opts.pref: The patient whose tumour carries an FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement, IDH1 mutation, BRAF V600E, HER2 amplification or overexpression, or MSI-high disease, and whose result is already in hand.
opts.avoid: Do not substitute a gene name for an alteration class, and do not read the single-arm survival figures as showing superiority over FOLFOX. Ivosidenib is the only randomised option and it met progression-free survival, not intention-to-treat overall survival.

opts.name: FOLFOX, where no driver is present
opts.when: ABC-06 gave median overall survival 6.2 versus 5.3 months against active symptom control, adjusted hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), p=0.031 — an absolute median gain of 0.9 months, open label, with grade 3–5 events in 69% versus 52% and three chemotherapy-related deaths (infection, acute kidney injury, febrile neutropenia).
opts.pref: A fit patient after progression on gemcitabine–platinum with no actionable alteration; the gain is clearest in survival rates, 25.9% versus 11.4% alive at 12 months, and albumin of 35 g/L or above was independently prognostic.
opts.avoid: A patient whose performance status or albumin makes 69% grade 3–5 toxicity the dominant outcome. Objective response was 5% and disease control 33%, so this is not a conversion strategy.
opts.note: 72 of 162 patients (44%) in ABC-06 had intrahepatic disease. Two delivery problems temper the result: 6 of 81 patients assigned FOLFOX never received it and 9 had only one cycle, while 8 of 81 in the control arm received off-study chemotherapy, and stratification errors found during data cleaning required a post hoc sensitivity analysis (adjusted hazard ratio 0.68, 0.49–0.95) to confirm the primary result. More FOLFOX patients were platinum resistant or refractory (67% versus 58%), which cuts against the treatment arm rather than for it. The trial predates molecular selection and first-line chemo-immunotherapy, both of which change who would now be offered FOLFOX second line.

alt.order: The order follows the roadmap's wording — use the matched agent where a driver is present, otherwise FOLFOX — not a survival comparison. FOLFOX carries the only randomised second-line evidence in this disease; the matched agents carry larger single-arm response and survival figures that have never been tested against chemotherapy. No randomised evidence establishes a sequence among the targeted options.
alt.flagnote: The molecular result should already be in hand at this point; if it is not, the omission in gate 2 has made this decision for you. Do not recycle immunotherapy without considering prior exposure.

avoid.t: Do not give liver-directed therapy for hepatic control while extrahepatic disease is progressing.
avoid.pref: If the liver is causing the symptoms and the extrahepatic disease is controlled, hepatic control can be discussed at the board with the goal stated explicitly.
avoid.avoid: Treating the liver while the disease progresses elsewhere spends liver reserve and time on an outcome that will not change the course.

gates.name: 7 · Which liver-directed treatment, and for what goal
crit: Treatment intent assigned before a device is chosen — cure, conversion or bridge, or hepatic control
Target geometry, liver reserve and biliary drainage assessed, not described from a report
What this institution can actually deliver confirmed — pump, personalised dosimetry, device and radiopharmaceutical availability, payer authorisation
Resection, local ablation and transplant compared at multidisciplinary review where appropriate
Intended outcome, why the alternatives do not fit, the systemic plan, the reassessment date and the next action all recorded
gates.ask: What am I trying to achieve in this liver, and which device actually achieves it here?

standard.t: Assign the treatment intent before choosing a device. Curative intent means an attempt to eradicate all known cancer; it does not establish a cure rate.
standard.pref: Every liver-directed decision. Local control, complete radiographic response, complete pathologic necrosis in a treated lesion, and overall survival are different outcomes; conflating hepatic control with cure is the commonest reasoning error here. Bridge and downstaging preserve a later transplant or resection opportunity and are recorded separately from definitive local treatment.
standard.avoid: Do not use a universal ablation > SBRT > Y90 > TACE > HAI > histotripsy ladder, and do not treat an upfront alternative chosen because of anatomy or organ reserve as a post-progression second line.
standard.note: The categories in the selector are a clinical synthesis, not a new formal evidence-grading system.

opts.name: Resection
opts.when: Goal: curative. Standard in the selector. Fits R0 achievable, liver-confined, adequate remnant and biliary drainage, fit patient.
opts.pref: The established curative standard whenever the anatomy and the reserve allow it — gate 3.
opts.avoid: Multifocal disease; nodal disease beyond the regional basin; inadequate remnant; any extrahepatic disease.

opts.name: Hepatic arterial infusion
opts.when: Goal: hepatic control or conversion. Preferred for a defined phenotype. Fits liver-confined unresectable disease, favourable arterial anatomy, with durable hepatic control or conversion as the stated goal. NCCN permits HAI in trials or experienced centres for carefully selected patients.
opts.pref: An approved expert programme with pump and arterial expertise, biliary toxicity monitoring and systemic coverage; it can be considered early rather than as a generic second line.
opts.avoid: No dedicated pump programme; extrahepatic disease; unrelieved biliary obstruction. Grade 4 toxicity requiring withdrawal occurred in 11% of the phase 2 cohort.

opts.name: SBRT or proton therapy
opts.when: Goal: selected definitive or consolidative local treatment. Reasonable consideration. Fits localized inoperable disease; cure evidence limited. Some of the evidence uses longer hypofractionated photon or proton schedules, not only 3–5-fraction SBRT.
opts.pref: May be selected directly on geometry and reserve; an unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite. Requires adequate liver reserve, biliary drainage and safe gastrointestinal and biliary doses.
opts.avoid: Insufficient uninvolved liver; unrelieved biliary obstruction; overlapping prior dose; refractory ascites. For bulky unresectable disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default.

opts.name: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation
opts.when: Goal: hepatic control. Reasonable consideration. Fits liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Y90 may also be used in a planned conversion strategy.
opts.pref: Selected hepatic-dominant disease where selective delivery and reserve are adequate, with personalised dosimetry and the systemic plan running alongside.
opts.avoid: Substituted for systemic therapy; used while extrahepatic disease progresses; inadequate future remnant or unsafe shunt fraction. Cirrhosis is the hard stop for radioembolisation plus chemotherapy — hepatic failure in 75% of cirrhotic patients, irreversible in 5 of 12.
opts.note: Evidence is heterogeneous and generally nonrandomised; no proven preferred sequence exists among TACE, Y90, HAI and ablative radiotherapy. Personalised dosimetry capability and payer authorisation are local dependencies.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: Goal: potentially curative intent in a narrow group. Reasonable consideration. Fits solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin; EASL-ILCA is narrower at under 2 cm. Central ducts often limit feasibility.
opts.pref: A small lesion when resection is unsuitable, with all disease treated to a safe margin and no uncontrolled nodal or distant disease; also at a first intrahepatic recurrence, where microwave ablation gave median overall survival 29.8 versus 34.0 months against repeat resection (HR 0.89, p=0.31) with major complications in 5.5% versus 31.3%.
opts.avoid: No safe margin, central bile duct injury risk, or unaddressed disease. Evidence is mainly retrospective and weaker than in hepatocellular carcinoma or colorectal liver metastases; do not extrapolate to large or multifocal iCCA. Document why the patient fits the narrower evidence base.
opts.note: At recurrence, repeat resection gave better disease-free survival in four strata: large-duct subtype, no complication at the initial resection, a disease-free interval under 12 months, and a margin under 5 mm. Read the recurrence comparison as the authors do: the 4-month difference in median overall survival was not significant but they call it clinically noteworthy and state the study cannot exclude a real difference, 18.0% of the cohort was lost to follow-up and censored, treatment was chosen by tumour board and patient preference, the repeat-resection arm was only 119 patients, and liver function and quality of life — the outcomes that would most favour ablation — were not measured. All ten centres were Chinese tertiary hospitals with operators averaging a decade of independent ablation experience, so the 5.5% major complication rate may not transfer.

opts.name: Liver transplantation
opts.when: Goal: total clearance. Trial or registry only. The best-characterised setting is a single tumour of 2 cm or less first diagnosed on cirrhotic explant pathology, most having been seen before transplant as presumed hepatocellular carcinoma — 15 patients in the index series, and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma was excluded from it.
opts.pref: Only inside a formally approved protocol with review-board approval and registry entry — gate 10.
opts.avoid: Multifocal or larger disease outside a protocol; any extrahepatic disease; no registry entry. A technical response does not establish transplant eligibility.

opts.name: Histotripsy
opts.when: Investigational oncologic role: no tumour-specific curative evidence in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Consider only under a prospective trial or institutional registry, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review.
opts.pref: Nothing outside a protocol. In the one-year update of the pivotal experience, local control was 63.4% on the primary assessment versus 90% post hoc in 47 patients with 52 tumours.
opts.avoid: FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation. Be particularly cautious around central biliary structures and prior instrumentation; a bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based.

standard.order: Intent, target geometry, liver reserve and what the institution can deliver choose the modality — not a hierarchy of evidence, because none exists. No randomised trial compares any two of these in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and none has been tested against a modern chemo-immunotherapy backbone. This order reproduces the roadmap's own selector table and carries no survival claim; resection is first because it is the established curative standard, and transplantation and histotripsy are last because both are protocol-only.
standard.flagnote: Unresolved decisions 1, 2, 6 and 7 all live here: whether the programme runs a hepatic arterial infusion service, which modality is first choice for unresectable liver-confined disease, the liver-function thresholds that bar each modality, and whether ablation is acceptable and in whom. The dependency flags the roadmap uses beyond demonstrated expertise — personalised dosimetry, device and radiopharmaceutical availability, payer authorisation and transplant timing — are local feasibility questions, not evidence questions.

alt.t: Record the decision in the form the registry can audit: intended outcome, why the alternatives fit or do not fit, the systemic-treatment plan, the reassessment date and the next action.
alt.pref: Every liver-directed case, because the unresolved questions above can only be answered from the programme's own data — modality, goal, hepatic progression-free survival and change in liver function.
alt.avoid: A note that records the device but not the goal makes the case useless for the registry and leaves the next team unable to tell a bridge from a definitive treatment.

avoid.t: Do not treat a complete local response as cure, or as a transplant exception.
avoid.pref: Reassess at 8–12 weeks allowing for the delayed response pattern after radiation-based therapy; nonprogression is not treatment failure.
avoid.avoid: A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception, and a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility.

gates.name: 8 · Adjuvant therapy after resection
crit: Macroscopically complete resection with curative intent, R0 or R1
Recovered enough to start within 16 weeks of surgery, with performance status and organ function to match
Node-positive or R1 disease, where the discussion carries most weight
A patient who wants to know what the trial actually showed before deciding
gates.ask: Do I offer capecitabine, and what do I tell this patient the trial showed?

standard.t: Have the adjuvant conversation with the numbers in front of you: BILCAP's intention-to-treat primary analysis did not meet statistical significance — median overall survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months, adjusted hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097.
standard.pref: Every patient being offered capecitabine. Significance appeared in the prespecified intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, tumour grade and sex (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.92, p=0.010) and in the per-protocol analysis (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.97, p=0.028); the trial was unmasked. Say both halves.
standard.avoid: Do not present it as settled. Only 84 of 447 patients (19%) had intrahepatic disease and the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, so the iCCA-specific benefit is unproven; LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup, while EASL-ILCA cites an iCCA hazard ratio of 0.65 — the best of the subtypes — and still grades the recommendation on a trial that was negative on intention to treat.
standard.note: Lymphadenectomy was not mandated for intrahepatic patients in BILCAP, yet nodal status is one of the covariates that turns the sensitivity analysis positive. Recurrence-free survival favoured capecitabine over the first 24 months (median 24.4 versus 17.5 months, adjusted hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.98, p=0.033) with no difference from 24 to 60 months (hazard ratio 1.48, 0.80–2.77, p=0.21), which the authors read as deferred rather than prevented recurrence. Recruitment ran nearly nine years with no fully defined analysis plan at the outset and the monitoring committee had to reset the event target when survival on observation proved far better than assumed. Two guideline readings of the same subgroup conflict and should not be presented as two datasets: LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup while EASL-ILCA cites an iCCA hazard ratio of 0.65 as the best of the subtypes — both are unpowered subgroup estimates from the trial that was negative on intention to treat. NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while acknowledging the nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; our Reasonable consideration is deliberately more cautious and requires explicit multidisciplinary ratification (alignment worksheet, area 11).

alt.t: Offer adjuvant capecitabine for 6 months as a reasonable consideration, not an obligation.
alt.pref: The fit patient after R0 or R1 resection, particularly node-positive or R1 disease, who has heard the trial endpoints and wants treatment. AASLD 2023 says capecitabine should be considered for all patients with cholangiocarcinoma and BSG 2023 recommends considering 24 weeks (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).
alt.avoid: A patient for whom the toxicity outweighs an unproven site-specific gain: grade 3 or worse events affected 44% of the 213 treated patients, most often hand-foot syndrome (20%), 32% stopped for toxicity and only 55% completed all eight cycles. Serious adverse events were 21% versus 10% on observation.
alt.note: Downgraded from B. The trial that supports it did not meet its primary intention-to-treat endpoint (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04, p=0.097), only 84 of 447 patients (19%) had intrahepatic disease and it was not powered for site-specific effects, so for this pathway the benefit is an unpowered subgroup of a negative trial. ACTICCA-1 has not reported. Our label sits closest to LCSGJ 2022's weak recommendation and is more cautious than AASLD 2023, BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA, each of which grades the recommendation strong. Whether it moves to Standard is unresolved decision 3.

alt.t: Discuss adjuvant chemoradiotherapy case by case at tumour board after an R1 or node-positive resection; it is not routine.
alt.pref: A margin or nodal result that genuinely changes the local-failure risk, discussed as a one-off decision with the radiation oncologist present.
alt.avoid: In intrahepatic disease the support is retrospective only, and BSG 2023 confines its recommendation for chemoradiotherapy after an R1 resection to extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer (alignment worksheet, area 11). Do not make it a standing rule for R1 iCCA.

avoid.pref: PRODIGE-12 was negative on both co-primary endpoints: relapse-free survival 30.4 versus 18.5 months, hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), p=0.48, and median time to definitive quality-of-life deterioration 31.8 versus 32.1 months, hazard ratio 1.28 (0.73–2.26), p=0.39; overall survival numerically favoured surveillance (median 75.8 versus 50.8 months, hazard ratio 1.08, 0.70–1.66).
avoid.avoid: Grade 3 toxicity affected 62% and grade 4 11%, with grade 3 peripheral sensory neuropathy in 18%. Intrahepatic patients were 86 of 194 (44%) and their relapse-free survival hazard ratio was 0.718 (0.431–1.196), so this is not a population mismatch excuse. Say what kind of negative it is: the trial was powered for a hazard ratio of 0.60 on 126 events, its medians fell on a plateau of the curves, and salvage differed sharply by arm (40 of 41 surveillance relapses received gemcitabine-based salvage versus 9 of 33 after GEMOX), so this is a failed superiority trial in a lower-risk population than BILCAP (13% R1 and 38% node-positive, against 38% and 47%) rather than a demonstration that adjuvant therapy does nothing.

avoid.t: Do not offer S-1 as the adjuvant option here, and do not use BCAT to argue against adjuvant therapy in intrahepatic disease.
avoid.pref: ASCOT met its primary endpoint — 3-year overall survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, stratified hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.51–0.94) — but relapse-free survival did not reach significance (hazard ratio 0.80, 0.61–1.04, p=0.088) with the curves crossing at 6 years, the analysis was done at 179 deaths, 62.8% of the 285 prespecified events, and the observation arm did far better than the hypothesised 47%. It was conducted entirely in Japan and S-1 is not available in the United States; only 58 of 440 patients (13%) had intrahepatic disease and that subgroup's hazard ratio, 0.75 (95% CI 0.30–1.89), is uninformative.
avoid.avoid: BCAT found no benefit for gemcitabine (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.70–1.45) but enrolled only resected extrahepatic bile duct cancer — intrahepatic disease was not eligible — which is why EASL-ILCA excluded it when answering the adjuvant question for iCCA. It is also underpowered on its own terms: recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, and the authors calculate only a 2.8% probability the result would have reached significance even with the planned 189 deaths. Neither trial can be quoted as evidence that adjuvant therapy is futile.

gates.name: 9 · First line and beyond for advanced disease
crit: Unresectable or metastatic disease, treated with systemic intent
Performance status, renal and hepatic function and contraindications to checkpoint inhibition assessed, including any prior adjuvant therapy
Progression on first-line gemcitabine–platinum, with the molecular result already in hand
Trial eligibility checked — at diagnosis and again at each progression
gates.ask: Is this patient fit for the full regimen, and what comes next when it fails?

standard.t: Cisplatin–gemcitabine with a checkpoint inhibitor is the first-line standard: ABC-02 established the backbone (overall survival 11.7 versus 8.1 months, hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.80), durvalumab added a hazard ratio of 0.80 and pembrolizumab 0.83.
standard.pref: Either combination is acceptable and the roadmap does not rank them; no trial compares them, so the choice is made on toxicity profile, schedule and access. ESMO 2024 recommends both [I, A] and states no biomarker favours one checkpoint inhibitor over the other.
standard.avoid: Do not read the backbone trial as an iCCA trial. The three trials differ sharply in how much of their population was actually intrahepatic: 80 of 410 patients (20%) in ABC-02, 383 of 685 (55.9%) in TOPAZ-1 and 633 of 1069 (59%) in KEYNOTE-966 — the last enriched because tumour tissue was mandatory and intrahepatic tumours are easier to sample. The modern figures are the ones that apply to this clinic; ABC-02's 11.7 months rests on a population in which gallbladder cancer was the largest single site at 36%, with a median follow-up of only 8.2 months, scans at weeks 12 and 24 by RECIST 1.0, and no molecular selection.
standard.note: In both chemo-immunotherapy trials the intrahepatic subgroup carried the effect — hazard ratio 0.76 in each — which is the opposite of the adjuvant picture in gate 8, where intrahepatic patients were a small minority. The absolute gains are small: 1.3 months of median survival with durvalumab and 1.8 with pembrolizumab, both bought with immune toxicity and, in KEYNOTE-966, more treatment-related deaths and no quality-of-life gain. The claim that the two are interchangeable is an indirect comparison across trials that differ in chemotherapy duration, geography and population; ESMO states no biomarker or efficacy difference separates them, and no randomised comparison exists.

standard.t: Performance status, renal and hepatic function, contraindications to checkpoint inhibition and prior therapy determine whether the full regimen is appropriate and at what intensity; any modification is recorded with its reason.
standard.pref: Every patient, before the first cycle. Both pivotal trials enrolled only ECOG 0–1 patients, so the standard assumes a patient fit for it.
standard.avoid: Do not quietly drop a component without recording why. BSG 2023 regards oxaliplatin substitution in renal impairment and gemcitabine alone in poor performance status as reasonable; our roadmap leaves the choice to the treating oncologist, and whether to name defaults is a ratification item.
standard.note: Clinical trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression. Standard, grade D.

alt.t: At progression, use the matched agent where a driver is present and FOLFOX where none is; recognise that those are different kinds of evidence.
alt.pref: ABC-06 is the only randomised second-line evidence: FOLFOX 6.2 versus 5.3 months against active symptom control, adjusted hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), with 12-month survival 25.9% versus 11.4%. The matched agents report larger response and survival figures from single-arm trials and have never been compared with chemotherapy.
alt.avoid: Do not treat the single-arm figures as comparative survival data, and do not expect a response-driven surgical opportunity from ivosidenib (response 2%) or from any of these agents. There is no randomised evidence establishing a sequence among the targeted options.
alt.note: ABC-06's benefit is an absolute median gain of 0.9 months and cost grade 3–5 toxicity in 69% versus 52% and three chemotherapy-related deaths; 44% of its patients had intrahepatic disease, and stratification errors discovered in data cleaning required a post hoc sensitivity analysis to confirm the result.

alt.t: Move to symptom-focused care when the reassessment answers that question, and make that an explicit tumour-board decision rather than a default.
alt.pref: The patient in whom the next line would buy toxicity rather than time. Biliary function is monitored alongside the disease throughout: liver biochemistry at every assessment, and a defined route for early detection of stent blockage.
alt.avoid: Do not let symptom-focused care mean no biliary care — BSG 2023 attributes the better-than-expected survival in the ABC-06 active-symptom-control arm to proactive treatment of biliary obstruction and infection. New jaundice, a rising bilirubin or cholangitis is evaluated promptly and does not wait for the next scheduled scan.

avoid.t: Do not recycle immunotherapy without considering prior exposure, and do not reach for a static second-line drug list instead of the molecular result.
avoid.pref: Confirm biomarker, line, label and access with oncology; NCCN states that treatment selection depends on previous regimen, somatic molecular testing results and extent of liver dysfunction.
avoid.avoid: Our position deliberately expands the molecular branch to the edition's matched options rather than a short static list (alignment worksheet, area 14).

gates.name: 10 · Transplant candidate
crit: Biopsy-proven solitary unresectable iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA
Tumour 3 cm or less, with underlying cirrhosis
Locoregional or systemic therapy received
Six months from diagnosis or last treatment with tumour stability on serial scans — still 3 cm or less, no new lesions, no extrahepatic disease
A formally approved trial or prospective registry protocol open, with review-board approval and registry entry
gates.ask: Is this patient inside the narrow phenotype, and do we have a protocol to put them on?

standard.t: Treat transplantation for known intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma as trial or prospective registry only: protocol, review-board approval and registry entry are prerequisites, not formalities.
standard.pref: This is our added institutional restriction, and it is a judgement about graft stewardship rather than an evidence finding. It sits closest to AASLD 2023 (research protocols only) and BSG 2023 (prospective national protocol), and is stricter than OPTN 2025 and ILTS-ILCA 2024, which both support consideration for cirrhotic, unresectable, biopsy-proven tumours of 3 cm or less after a period of stability.
standard.avoid: Do not state that iCCA has no exception route — OPTN review-board guidance now describes one — and do not apply the perihilar neoadjuvant or stricture pathway to intrahepatic disease. LCSGJ 2022 states iCCA is generally not an indication for transplantation at all.
standard.note: ILTS-ILCA 2024 — published twice, in Liver Transplantation 2025 and Liver Cancer 2026 — grades the cirrhotic ≤3 cm recommendation moderate evidence, moderate strength, and confines non-cirrhotic disease to investigational protocols after at least 6 months of stability on systemic therapy (moderate evidence, weak strength). It also makes biopsy mandatory to confirm iCCA, assess differentiation and exclude mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma, and finds no evidence for using molecular profiling to select candidates.
