Every one of its iCCA recommendations rests on low or moderate evidence and is graded weak or moderate, and the consensus reports modern 5-year post-transplant outcomes spanning 25–73% overall survival and 29–82% recurrence-free survival, almost entirely from single-centre retrospective series — a range too wide to support a selection rule. It makes no recommendation on allocation priority, exception points or acceptable waitlist dropout, and reached no agreement on large, locally advanced or non-cirrhotic disease.

standard.t: Where a protocol exists, the allocation route is a nonstandard MMaT-3 exception: select the CCA diagnosis form and submit a written narrative to the Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board.
standard.pref: iCCA, neuroendocrine liver metastasis and colorectal liver metastasis all go through nonstandard review; hepatocellular carcinoma and perihilar cholangiocarcinoma have standardised routes. Clinical transplant candidacy and local protocol approval remain separate from allocation eligibility.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the guidance as policy: OPTN Policy 9.5 defines standardised exceptions, and the Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology document is review-board guidance, not OPTN Policy or a clinical standard of care.
standard.note: MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not one fixed national score; under Policy 9.4.E an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15, and exceptions generally require 90-day extensions (9.4.C). The coordinator records source version, eligibility dates, request and extension dates, imaging, laboratory values and a named renewal owner; transplant leadership signs the allocation assessment. Required allocation record: diagnosis and histology; baseline burden and AFP/CEA where applicable; primary and last-treatment dates; serial response imaging; extrahepatic staging; request and extension dates; score route; named coordinator and physician sign-off. Reassess at progression, recurrence, new extrahepatic findings and each extension.

standard.t: Read the supporting evidence for what it is: in 15 patients with a single tumour of 2 cm or less, the 5-year recurrence risk was 18% versus 61% for larger or multifocal disease, with 5-year survival 65% versus 45% — in explants where the cancer was first diagnosed on explant pathology.
standard.pref: Quote it when the question is the prognosis of a very small intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma discovered on an explant removed for another reason, which is the population it describes: 15 patients, 7 of them (47%) entirely incidental, from 17 centres and 25,016 transplants.
standard.avoid: Crucially these tumours were recognised as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma only at explant, not selected for transplantation, so the result cannot be read as licensing transplantation of known disease. Fifteen patients leaves very few still at risk at 5 years and the authors call the 3- and 5-year rates encouraging rather than established. No lymphadenectomy was performed because iCCA was not suspected, central pathology review was possible in only 55 of 81 cases (68%), each of 17 centres used its own pathologist so number and size may be understaged, and recurrence was driven by microvascular invasion (HR 4.7, 1.6–13.8) and poor differentiation (HR 6.1, 1.9–20.2) — neither of which is knowable before transplant.
standard.note: Three limits of this series bear directly on how it is cited here. It studied tumours of 2 cm or less, not 3 cm: the ceiling in our criteria comes from EASL-ILCA, OPTN and ILTS-ILCA, and inside this series it rests on a 6-patient subgroup of single 2.1–3 cm, not poorly differentiated tumours whose 5-year survival was 61%. It required no period of disease stability on therapy and could not have — the diagnosis was made on the explant, bridging chemoembolisation, ablation or ethanol injection was permitted but was not a selection test, and 7 of the 15 (47%) were incidental findings after transplant for decompensated cirrhosis. And it excluded mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma within a nodule outright, analysing the 33 explants with separate iCCA and hepatocellular nodules as a separate group outside the 48-patient study population, so it reports no outcome at all for the mixed tumours our gate criteria admit. The wider literature is no firmer: a 2020 meta-analysis of 18 studies and 355 patients gave pooled 5-year survival of 42% and pooled recurrence 43%, with 5-year recurrence-free survival 67% for single tumours of 2 cm or less versus 34% for more advanced disease, and a propensity-matched National Cancer Database comparison found transplant and resection within a few percentage points of each other at 5 years — whose authors argued resection should remain preferred for localised iCCA.

opts.name: Keep all transplantation for known iCCA inside a research protocol (current roadmap position)
opts.when: v0.6 cites the OPTN guidance without changing the label: Trial or prospective registry only.
opts.pref: A programme that is not prepared to commit the organ, the registry infrastructure and the transplant-oncology selection expertise that the alternative requires.
opts.avoid: It leaves a patient who meets every OPTN criterion without a route here, which is the cost that has to be stated openly when the decision is ratified.

opts.name: Open a defined, registry-tracked pathway on the OPTN 2025 and ILTS-ILCA 2024 criteria
opts.when: Biopsy-proven, unresectable, solitary iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA of 3 cm or less, in cirrhosis, after a period of observed radiographic stability, scored at MMaT-3. Note that ILTS-ILCA attaches no duration to that period for the cirrhotic ≤3 cm phenotype; the six-month figure in our criteria comes from its separate, weakly graded route for non-cirrhotic locally advanced disease and from the prospective protocol below.
opts.pref: The route both documents describe; OPTN 2025 gives the review board defined criteria and ILTS-ILCA 2024 reports broad community agreement on the cirrhotic ≤3 cm phenotype.
opts.avoid: Every iCCA recommendation in the ILTS-ILCA consensus rests on low or moderate evidence and is graded weak or moderate, and the 3 cm threshold is carried forward from a small retrospective series of explant-discovered tumours whose own cut-off was 2 cm — the single-centre series behind it span 5-year survival of 25–73%. EASL-ILCA concedes the 3 cm figure is more permissive than the 2 cm cut-off used in the series and trials it cites, and ILTS-ILCA notes the ceiling mirrors the June 2024 OPTN review-board criteria rather than any new data. The consensus also recommends nothing on allocation priority or acceptable waitlist dropout, which makes the criterion hard to act on where iCCA earns no priority.

opts.name: Locally advanced disease selected on sustained stability, under protocol
opts.when: The prospective Houston Methodist–MD Anderson protocol: 21 patients referred, 12 listed, 6 transplanted after a mandatory 6 months of radiographic stability on gemcitabine-based therapy. Post-transplant survival 100% at 1 year and 83.3% at 3 and 5 years, but recurrence-free survival 50% at 1, 3 and 5 years.
opts.pref: This is the only prospective experience in locally advanced disease, and it is where the 6-month stability requirement in the OPTN biology clock comes from.
opts.avoid: Six patients, no control arm, no power calculation and no trial registration — it was run as a centre policy. Median cumulative tumour diameter was 14.2 cm with no patient under 5 cm, and 3 of 6 recurred at a median of 7.6 months. Two of the six had stable extrahepatic lesions before transplant that proved to be metastases and a third recurred after perihilar fat invasion found only on explant, so the authors concede more aggressive pre-transplant sampling is needed. Only 9 patients were listed in 6 years, so the strategy reaches a very small fraction of referrals. Selecting for 6 months of chemotherapy stability may itself be selecting indolent biology, and without a comparator it cannot be known whether these patients would have done as well on continued chemotherapy. Half the grafts were extended-criteria livers refused by every other centre — used because no MELD exception existed at the time — so the approach is not reproducible where such organs are not available. ILTS-ILCA confines non-cirrhotic locally advanced disease to investigational protocols with a weak recommendation.

alt.order: These are not ranked by survival — no comparison between them exists, and a randomised comparison is not feasible. The first is the roadmap's current position, the second is the question the group is being asked to decide, and the third is the protocol experience that both the OPTN biology clock and the sceptics draw on. Area 15 of the alignment worksheet asks explicitly which of the first two the programme adopts.
alt.flagnote: Unresolved decision 5: does the programme open an intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma transplant protocol? The evidence is retrospective and confined to small tumours first diagnosed on explant pathology, most seen before transplant as presumed hepatocellular carcinoma; graft stewardship is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question. Transplant timing and payer authorisation are local dependencies.

alt.t: If intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is found in an explant removed for another indication, enter the patient into structured surveillance and the registry.
alt.pref: This is the population the published outcomes actually describe, and it is where the programme's own data will come from.
alt.avoid: Immunosuppression minimisation and adjuvant therapy are individualised; there is no comparative evidence to support either, so do not present a protocol where none exists.

avoid.t: Do not transplant multifocal or larger disease outside a protocol, and never with any extrahepatic disease or without registry entry.
avoid.pref: The eligible phenotype is narrow and explicit — solitary, 3 cm or less, cirrhosis, treated, six months stable — but say where each limb comes from: the size ceiling and the stability requirement are guideline and review-board criteria, not findings of the explant series, whose own cut-off was 2 cm and which required no stability at all.
avoid.avoid: In the explant series, larger or multifocal tumours recurred in 61% by 5 years with 45% survival, and the crude recurrence split was 2 of 15 versus 18 of 33. A broader resection or systemic-treatment population must not be treated as exception-eligible.

avoid.t: Do not treat mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma as eligible for the hepatocellular carcinoma exception pathway.
avoid.pref: Treat it as biliary disease for transplant purposes unless a protocol states otherwise, and flag it to the transplant team explicitly; OPTN 2025 routes mixed HCC-iCCA through the same nonstandard request as iCCA.
avoid.avoid: ILTS-ILCA makes biopsy mandatory partly to exclude a mixed tumour, and reviews note that pooling mixed tumours with pure iCCA can make survival and recurrence look falsely favourable when the dominant phenotype is hepatocellular. The index explant series excluded mixed tumours within a nodule entirely, so there is no transplant outcome dataset for this phenotype to argue from in either direction.

quickref.title: Molecular alterations that change treatment
quickref.intro: Ordered at the diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease, not at second-line progression; turnaround is two to four weeks.
rows: Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum. Response 37% and 42%, median overall survival 17.5 and 21.7 months. Both single-arm; neither compared with second-line chemotherapy.

Ivosidenib. Met progression-free survival (2.7 versus 1.4 months, HR 0.37); final intention-to-treat overall survival 10.3 versus 7.5 months, HR 0.79, p=0.09, not significant with crossover permitted. Response 2% — position it on progression-free survival grounds only.
Dabrafenib plus trametinib. Single-arm, 43 patients, response 51% by investigator and 47% by independent review, interim analysis.

Zanidatamab. Single-arm; final analysis of 80 ERBB2-amplified patients gave confirmed response 41.3% and median overall survival 15.5 months, concentrated in IHC 3+ (51.6% versus 1 of 18 at IHC 2+; post hoc).
Checkpoint blockade, consistent with tumour-agnostic practice.
NTRK fusion, RET fusion, other actionable
Capture on the same broad panel so a later line is not delayed by re-testing. Reasonable consideration, grade C.
quickref.foot: Match the alteration class reported, not the gene name: other alterations in these same genes are not interchangeable with the ones studied and go to molecular-oncology review first (Standard, grade D). Use circulating tumour DNA when tissue is inadequate or biopsy would delay treatment, but a negative plasma result does not exclude a target and should prompt tissue testing where it would change management. No randomised evidence establishes a sequence among these options.

quickref.title: Resectability, as the roadmap defines it
quickref.intro: A surgical determination made by a hepatobiliary surgeon, not a radiological impression, reassessed whenever the disease or the liver changes.
rows: Favours: solitary or clustered disease clearable with an R0 margin and an adequate functional remnant. Against: multifocal disease across both lobes; satellite pattern implying field disease.
Favours: inflow, outflow and biliary drainage preservable or reconstructable. Against: encasement precluding reconstruction; bilateral second-order biliary involvement.

Favours: no nodal disease, or regional nodes resectable within the standard basin — lymphadenectomy is part of the operation and informs adjuvant decisions. Against: nodal disease beyond the regional basin, including retroperitoneal or coeliac stations.
Favours: no extrahepatic disease. Against: any extrahepatic disease — this moves the pathway to systemic and molecularly directed therapy.
Favours: adequate reserve and performance status. Against: parenchymal disease or reserve that makes the necessary resection unsafe.
quickref.foot: Three gaps to know about. 'Regional basin' is undefined in v0.6; AASLD 2023 draws the line at nodal metastasis beyond the hepatoduodenal and gastrohepatic ligaments. Numeric reserve rules remain specialty-approved local implementation, and the roadmap is silent on portal hypertension, which AASLD 2023 names a contraindication to resection. Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure — resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large, and BSG 2023 puts that threshold at a remnant above 50%; cholangitis is drained without waiting.

quickref.title: Transplant eligibility — the nonstandard MMaT-3 route
quickref.intro: All of these are required by the described route, and our programme adds a protocol requirement on top.
rows: Biopsy-proven solitary unresectable iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA.

Six months from diagnosis or last treatment with tumour stability: still 3 cm or less, no new lesions, no extrahepatic disease. Record both diagnosis and last-treatment dates and the serial scans that establish the interval — a response on one scan is insufficient.
Imaging every three months showing tumour still 3 cm or less with no extrahepatic disease; track the general 90-day extension cycle with a named renewal owner.
Nonstandard MMaT-3 exception: CCA diagnosis form plus a written narrative to the Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board. An MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 (Policy 9.4.E).
A formally approved trial or prospective registry protocol, plus expert transplant-oncology selection. This is an additional institutional restriction, not an OPTN requirement.
quickref.foot: MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not one fixed national score, and the supplied document is review-board guidance, not OPTN policy or a clinical standard of care. Six months is also the period of radiographic stability the Houston Methodist–MD Anderson prospective series required before listing: 6 of 21 referred patients were transplanted, with 5-year survival 83.3% but recurrence-free survival 50% and a median cumulative tumour diameter of 14.2 cm. Poor differentiation is associated with worse outcome in the guidance footnote — a clinical selection concern, not a separately stated automatic exclusion. A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception.

quickref.title: BILCAP, as published
quickref.intro: The trial the adjuvant capecitabine recommendation rests on. Read the primary analysis, not the habit.
rows: 447 patients with resected biliary tract cancer: 84 (19%) intrahepatic, 128 (29%) hilar, 156 (35%) lower common bile duct, 79 (18%) muscle-invasive gallbladder; 38% R1 and 47% node-positive.
Median overall survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months, adjusted hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097. Not significant.
Adjusted for nodal status, tumour grade and sex: hazard ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.55–0.92), p=0.010.
Hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.58–0.97), p=0.028. The trial was unmasked.
24.4 versus 17.5 months, hazard ratio 0.75 over the first 24 months, with no difference from 24 to 60 months — the authors read this as deferred rather than prevented recurrence.
Grade 3 or worse in 44% of the 213 treated, most often hand-foot syndrome (20%); 55% completed all eight cycles, 46% needed a dose reduction and 32% stopped for toxicity.

ASCOT: 3-year survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, hazard ratio 0.69 — Japan only, S-1 unavailable in the United States, 13% intrahepatic. PRODIGE-12: negative for gemcitabine–oxaliplatin, grade 3–4 toxicity 73%. BCAT: no benefit for gemcitabine (hazard ratio 1.01) in extrahepatic bile duct cancer only, iCCA not eligible.
quickref.foot: Local label: Reasonable consideration, grade B. NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while acknowledging the nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 treat it as standard, and LCSGJ 2022 makes a weak recommendation and reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup. Lymphadenectomy was not mandated for intrahepatic patients, yet nodal status is one of the covariates that turns the sensitivity analysis positive. Offer capecitabine, discuss it with these numbers, and do not present it as settled — whether the label moves to Standard is unresolved decision 3.

honest.t: Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure, particularly when a major hepatectomy is contemplated. Cholangitis is drained without waiting for that discussion.
honest.why: Standard, grade D. No comparative outcome data were identified for intrahepatic disease. The reasoning is mechanical rather than empirical: stent-related inflammation distorts the ductal extent that decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed, and drainage of the wrong side adds cholangitis risk and delay.

honest.t: Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, and record the entry dataset: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, regional nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology.
honest.why: Both are grade D. The work-up justification is that metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and that treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as iCCA is a recognised and consequential error — not that any study shows colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging or a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel changes outcomes. The recorded dataset is a documentation standard the programme has chosen so that resectability, candidacy and the registry can be audited; no comparative outcome evidence supports the particular list. CA 19-9 and CEA are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis, and AASLD 2023 states explicitly that an elevated CA 19-9 alone must not be used to diagnose cholangiocarcinoma.

honest.t: Match treatment to the alteration class reported, not to the gene name; other alterations in the same genes are not interchangeable and should be reviewed with a clinician experienced in molecular oncology before a matched agent is chosen.
honest.why: Standard, grade D. Locally reasonable and consistent with how the trials selected patients, but it is a consensus rule: no comparative data establish what happens when a non-canonical alteration is treated with a matched agent.

honest.t: Reassessment intervals: systemic therapy every 8–12 weeks by RECIST 1.1 with CA 19-9 as a supporting trend only; after resection every 3–6 months for 2 years then less frequently; after liver-directed therapy at 8–12 weeks allowing for the delayed response pattern; conversion intent at the pre-declared 2–3 month point, by formal surgical re-review rather than an imaging report alone.
honest.why: The response-assessment framework in this disease is expert consensus, not randomised evidence — grade C to D. NCCN states there are no data to support a specific surveillance schedule. Whether post-resection imaging should be fixed at 3-monthly, given that most recurrences are intrahepatic and some are re-resectable, or 6-monthly as most UK centres practise, is a ratification item (alignment worksheet, area 16).

honest.t: Biliary function is monitored alongside the disease: liver biochemistry at each assessment, and every patient with a biliary stent has a defined route for early detection of blockage. New jaundice, a rising bilirubin or cholangitis is evaluated promptly and does not wait for the next scheduled scan.
honest.why: Standard, grade D. Supported only indirectly — BSG 2023 attributes the better-than-expected survival of the ABC-06 active-symptom-control arm to proactive treatment of biliary obstruction and infection.

honest.t: The tumour board operating model, and the standing rule that trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression.
honest.why: These are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, reproduced unchanged across every disease roadmap so the programme has one operating standard rather than five: submission form, triage, stable agenda, urgent lane, required attendance, imaging reviewed rather than described, pathology pre-alerted, one recommendation with one owner and one reassessment date, documentation within one business day, registry closure. The trial-eligibility rule belongs to the same class. All are evidence grade D by construction — local policy choices with no comparative outcome evidence — and are labelled Standard because the programme has chosen them, not because trials support them. The eligibility rule is defensible in a disease where most of the molecularly matched evidence is single-arm, but no study shows that systematic eligibility checking improves outcome. Audit them for adherence, not for effectiveness.

honest.t: Thresholds barring each liver-directed modality by liver function, and the order in which the modalities are listed.
honest.why: No comparative data define the cut-offs; they are safety conventions. The one hard stop that does come from data is cirrhosis before radioembolisation with chemotherapy, where hepatic failure occurred in 9 of 12 cirrhotic patients (75%), irreversible in 5, against 5 of 29 (17%) without cirrhosis, all reversible — and every irreversible case had whole-liver treatment. Everything else, including the liver-function limits for ablation and for ablative radiotherapy, is convention. Unresolved decision 6, audited through decompensation after liver-directed therapy. The order itself carries no claim either. No randomised trial compares any two of hepatic arterial infusion, radioembolisation, chemoembolisation, ablative radiotherapy and thermal ablation in this disease, and none has been tested against a modern systemic backbone, so the sequence on the page reproduces the roadmap's table and the depth of each dataset rather than a hierarchy of evidence. Selection runs on treatment goal, target geometry, liver reserve and what the institution can deliver, and an upfront alternative chosen for anatomy or reserve is not a post-progression second line. Unresolved decisions 2, 6 and 7.

honest.t: Retain the local requirement for a formally approved trial or prospective registry protocol and expert transplant-oncology selection before any transplantation for known intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
honest.why: This is an additional institutional restriction, not an evidence finding. OPTN 2025 guidance and ILTS-ILCA 2024 both describe a route for cirrhotic, unresectable, biopsy-proven tumours of 3 cm or less after six months of stability; the roadmap declines to open it outside a protocol because graft stewardship is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question. Unresolved decision 5. What cannot honestly be given alongside it is an expected outcome. The published 5-year figures in iCCA span 25–73% overall survival and 29–82% recurrence-free survival, almost entirely from single-centre retrospective series, a range the ILTS-ILCA panel itself calls too wide to support a selection rule; almost every series describes iCCA found incidentally or misdiagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma, so none is an intention-to-treat result and waitlist dropout for progression is unmeasured. A propensity-matched National Cancer Database comparison put transplant and resection within a few percentage points of each other at 5 years, and its authors argued resection should remain preferred for localised disease.

honest.t: If intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is found in an explant removed for another indication, enter the patient into structured surveillance and the registry; immunosuppression minimisation and adjuvant therapy are individualised.
honest.why: Local policy. There is no comparative evidence for either immunosuppression minimisation or adjuvant therapy in this situation, and the published outcomes describe exactly this incidentally diagnosed population rather than a selected one.

honest.t: Mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma is out of scope for the hepatocellular carcinoma exception pathway: treat it as biliary disease for transplant purposes unless a protocol states otherwise, and flag it to the transplant team explicitly.
honest.why: Local policy, concordant with OPTN 2025, which routes mixed tumours through the same nonstandard request as iCCA, and with ILTS-ILCA 2024, which makes biopsy mandatory partly to exclude a mixed tumour. What is not known is how these patients do after transplantation. The index explant series excluded mixed tumours within a nodule outright and analysed the 33 explants with separate iCCA and hepatocellular nodules as a group outside its 48-patient study population, so it reports no outcome for them; the wider review literature notes that pooling mixed tumours with pure iCCA can make survival and recurrence look falsely favourable when the dominant phenotype is hepatocellular. The policy is therefore a precaution against an unquantified risk, not a reading of a dataset.

honest.t: Adjuvant capecitabine after resection of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
honest.why: BILCAP did not meet its primary endpoint. Intention-to-treat median overall survival was 51.1 versus 36.4 months with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097; significance appeared only in a prespecified sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, grade and sex (0.71, 0.55–0.92) and in the per-protocol analysis (0.75, 0.58–0.97), in an unmasked trial whose analysis plan was not fully defined at the outset. Intrahepatic patients were 84 of 447 (19%) and the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, so no iCCA-specific benefit has been shown. The two guideline readings of that subgroup contradict each other — LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit, EASL-ILCA cites a hazard ratio of 0.65 as the best of the subtypes — and they are not two datasets but two readings of one unpowered subgroup of a negative trial. What is actually known is that recurrence was deferred rather than prevented (no difference in recurrence-free survival from 24 to 60 months) and that 44% of treated patients had a grade 3 event, 32% stopped for toxicity and 55% finished all eight cycles. ACTICCA-1 has not reported. Our label is Reasonable consideration, grade C, and the conversation is the deliverable.

honest.t: The 3 cm tumour ceiling for a transplant referral.
honest.why: No study derived it. The series our page cites studied single tumours of 2 cm or less; EASL-ILCA concedes its own 3 cm figure is more permissive than the 2 cm cut-off used in the series and trials it cites, and ILTS-ILCA 2024 notes its ceiling mirrors the June 2024 OPTN review-board criteria rather than new data. Inside the index series the 2.1–3 cm band rests on 6 patients — single, not poorly differentiated tumours, 5-year survival 61%. A threshold nobody derived should be stated as a referral convention that the review board and the guidelines share, not as a size at which biology changes.

honest.t: Six months from diagnosis or last treatment with tumour stability, as a transplant criterion.
honest.why: The clock does not come from the evidence for the phenotype it is applied to. The explant series required no period of stability and could not have, because the diagnosis was made on the explant; bridging chemoembolisation, ablation or ethanol injection was permitted but was not a selection test, and 7 of its 15 very early patients (47%) were incidental findings after transplant for decompensated cirrhosis. ILTS-ILCA 2024 attaches no duration at all to the cirrhotic ≤3 cm recommendation — only 'a period of observation showing stability'. The six-month figure comes from its separate, weakly graded route for non-cirrhotic locally advanced disease and from the prospective Houston Methodist–MD Anderson protocol, where 6 months of radiographic stability on gemcitabine-based therapy was mandatory. Keeping it is defensible as a biology test; what is not known is whether six months is the right length, and the protocol's own authors concede that selecting for stability may simply be selecting indolent biology.

honest.t: First-line chemo-immunotherapy: the grade it carries in gate 5, and the choice between the two agents.
honest.why: Graded B here rather than A, because the trials that establish the regimen did not study this population. TOPAZ-1 was 86% metastatic and KEYNOTE-966 89%, both ECOG 0–1, and the TOPAZ-1 investigators state that the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use in liver-confined disease — which is exactly where the regimen is now borrowed. The absolute gains in the trials as run are 1.3 and 1.8 months of median survival, TOPAZ-1's proportional-hazards assumption was formally violated and it was reported at a prespecified interim analysis, and KEYNOTE-966 missed its prespecified boundaries for both progression-free survival and response. Grade A remains right for gate 9. The choice between them is not an evidence finding either. There is no randomised comparison; ESMO declares the two interchangeable on an indirect comparison across trials differing in chemotherapy duration (gemcitabine capped at eight cycles in TOPAZ-1, continued to progression in KEYNOTE-966), geography and size, and states that no clinical, biochemical or molecular biomarker favours one. Neither trial found a predictive biomarker: benefit did not track PD-L1 in either, MSI status was missing for about half of TOPAZ-1 and only 10 KEYNOTE-966 patients were MSI-high. Present the choice as toxicity profile, schedule and access.

honest.t: The matched targeted agents in gate 2, as a group.
honest.why: Only one of them comes from a randomised trial, and that trial was negative on intention-to-treat overall survival. ClarIDHy met progression-free survival (2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37) but final intention-to-treat survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (0.56–1.12), p=0.09, with 70% crossover; the frequently quoted 0.49 comes from a crossover-adjustment model that assumes the drug's effect is identical whenever given. Pemigatinib, futibatinib, zanidatamab and dabrafenib–trametinib are single-arm, all approved on single-arm data, and none has been compared with second-line chemotherapy; the pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy that makes their agent look better, since FGFR2-fusion disease itself carries longer survival from diagnosis. Every one is industry-sponsored with sponsor involvement in design, analysis and writing. What is known is response rate and duration in a selected population; what is not known is survival against the alternative. A related choice sits on the same table: our rows require that HER2, NTRK and RET findings be captured but do not name trastuzumab deruxtecan, entrectinib, larotrectinib or selpercatinib, which ESMO 2024 recommends on level III grade A. The reason to hesitate is assay definition and evidence level rather than availability — ESMO concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 status in biliary tract cancer and that no specific test can be recommended, while making two HER2-directed recommendations that depend on that undefined assay, and zanidatamab's own data are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite. Alignment worksheet, area 14.

honest.t: Hepatic arterial infusion as the strongest regional option.
honest.why: The phase 2 evidence is 38 treated patients at one institution, selected from 84 screened, with the comparison drawn from historical systemic series; the linked editorial judged the case for locoregional therapy in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma still unsettled without a randomised trial, and the authors themselves called for one. The retrospective comparison that gives 30.8 versus 18.4 months had all HAI patients surgically staged against 42% of a 26-patient comparator of whom only 30% received gemcitabine–cisplatin, so stage migration favours HAI; 44 of its 93 HAI patients came from earlier phase 2 trials, and it reports no pump complication or biliary toxicity rate at all. Conversion to curative-intent resection occurred in 8 of 236 patients (3%). Delivery is harder than the figures suggest: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months and 47% over the next 6, and grade 4 pump or arterial complications forced withdrawal in 11% of the lead-centre cohort and 30% of the 10-patient confirmatory cohort. The deciding variables for the programme are pump expertise, nursing infrastructure and case volume, not the evidence.

honest.t: Y90 radioembolisation as a conversion strategy.
honest.why: One single-arm phase 2 of 41 patients, run only at centres experienced with glass microspheres and part-funded by the microsphere manufacturer, with several authors as its consultants. Its 22% downstaging and 20% R0 rates describe a doubly selected cohort: 4 of 45 patients were excluded at the planning angiogram and 9 of 41 had major protocol deviations, leaving 32 per protocol. The authors state tumour-absorbed dose rather than a generic liver dose probably drives outcome, so the regimen does not transfer as written, and grade 3–4 toxicity affected 71%. Two patients whose disease stayed unresectable but controlled were offered transplant and both recurred, at 16 and 17 months. The confirmatory randomised SIRCCA trial has not reported.

honest.t: Ablative radiotherapy doses, and the 80.5 Gy figure.
honest.why: It is an association in a retrospective single-centre series of 79 patients in which only 19 received the high dose. Those 19 also had significantly smaller planning target volumes (median 415 versus 614 cm³, p=0.02), and the high doses arrived with breath-hold gating and daily diagnostic-quality CT image guidance after 2010, so anatomy, technique and era are all confounded with dose — patients treated after 2010 survived 50 versus 24 months. The prospective proton data are a safety and local-control signal, not a survival finding: the 39-patient iCCA cohort had no prespecified efficacy hypothesis, median delivered dose was 58.0 GyE against an intended 67.5, every local failure occurred below 60 GyE, local failures kept accruing past 2 years and 53.8% developed distant metastases. The randomised answer was deferred to NRG GI-001, which closed early for poor accrual. Treat the dose as a planning aspiration, not a threshold.

honest.t: Thermal ablation as an alternative to resection for a small tumour.
honest.why: The cohort that reports parity did not test our rule. Its entry criterion was Milan-equivalent — a single tumour up to 5 cm, or up to three each 3 cm or less — not the under-3 cm wording the page uses, and within it a 3–5 cm tumour was an independent risk factor for disease-free survival after ablation but not after resection. The equivalence headline comes from a post hoc split at 2017, where the later comparison was underpowered (p=0.129), and a nonsignificant difference is not equivalence; margin was measured by post-ablation CT or MR in one arm and on the specimen in the other, which the authors accept may bias the mediation result their conclusion rests on. Resection still outperformed ablation in patients under 60, with hepatolithiasis, with left-lobe tumours and with GGT above 50 U/L. The pooled meta-analysis behind the under-3 cm limit is 20 retrospective studies with I² up to 85%, publication bias on 3-year survival (Egger p=0.039), a dichotomised size variable and no individual patient data; pooled recurrence-free survival was 40.0% at 1 year and 19.2% at 3. The structural problem for a surgeon is different: ablation yields no specimen and no nodal dissection, so there is no pathological node status to drive the gate 8 decision, and node-negativity rests on imaging whose sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61%.

honest.t: Routine regional lymphadenectomy at every iCCA resection.
honest.why: No guideline recommends it on evidence of survival benefit. LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation on node dissection at all and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications; ESMO 2023 recommends routine hepatoduodenal-ligament dissection on level IV evidence; BSG 2023 says nothing about extent or node yield, which its own critics identify as a gap given that the adjuvant recommendation it then makes turns on nodal status; AASLD 2023 likewise makes no statement. Keeping it in every operation is a staging decision the programme has made so that the adjuvant conversation and the registry have a denominator, not a survival finding. Unresolved; audit the node yield, not the outcome.

honest.t: Two resectability criteria this page states but does not define: the regional nodal basin, and the liver-reserve limit.
honest.why: The basin is not defined in this version. AASLD 2023 draws the boundary at nodal metastasis beyond the hepatoduodenal and gastrohepatic ligaments and NCCN at beyond the porta hepatis; an undefined basin cannot be audited and two surgeons can reach opposite conclusions on the same scan. Clinical nodal staging is also insensitive here — reported sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61% — so the criterion is applied to an uncertain input. On the other side the roadmap is silent on portal hypertension, while AASLD 2023 names decompensated cirrhosis and portal hypertension as contraindications to resection and LCSGJ 2022 builds its whole algorithm on Child-Pugh class, sending Child-Pugh C to palliative care. No comparative data define numeric reserve thresholds in iCCA, so any local rule is a safety convention, which is why it stays specialty-approved local implementation rather than being asserted here. Alignment worksheet, areas 3 and 4.

honest.t: Conversion therapy with a declared reassessment, and the rates quoted for it.
honest.why: The 36.4% and 53% conversion rates are retrospective Japanese series quoted by LCSGJ 2022, which in the same document records no evidence of benefit for neoadjuvant chemotherapy and makes no recommendation; the denominators are not defined and those series report median survival of 24.1 months in converted patients against 25.7 months in those primarily resectable. AASLD 2023 states the role of neoadjuvant downstaging is not well defined and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Neither modern chemo-immunotherapy trial supports downstaging, since both were almost entirely metastatic. The prospective conversion numbers that do exist are small: 9 of 41 downstaged and 8 resected with Y90 plus chemotherapy, 4 of 38 with hepatic arterial infusion. What is defensible is the discipline — record the obstacle to R0, declare the reassessment date, hold a formal surgical re-review — not a conversion rate.

honest.t: Ordering broad molecular profiling at diagnosis rather than at progression.
honest.why: The argument is operational, not biological, and no study shows that ordering earlier improves outcome. What supports it is turnaround of two to four weeks against a second-line decision that cannot wait, plus the screening arithmetic: 783 patients screened to enrol 103 in FOENIX-CCA2, 1,206 prescreened to find 107 fusion-positive patients for FIGHT-202, and a BRAF V600E yield reported at 9% but nearer 5–7% in practice because sites entered known positives. Our grade B is lower than ESMO's level I grade A and BSG's strong recommendation on high-quality evidence; the obstacle in practice is payer authorisation and ordering discipline, which is why this is audited as a proportion rather than asserted as a standard. The plasma alternative is weaker than its headline figure suggests: the 87% quoted for plasma detection of an FGFR2 fusion comes from 83 of 95 FOENIX-CCA2 patients already known to be tissue-positive, so it measures concordance in a positive population, not the chance of finding a target de novo. No study in this disease reports the latter, and BSG 2023 notes DNA-based panels and most liquid biopsies are weaker at detecting fusions, so a negative plasma result in a patient whose management would change should prompt tissue testing rather than closing the question.

honest.t: Sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP, and reusing it for the gate 2 profile.
honest.why: The accuracy data are strong on their own terms — 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity against 44% for pathology, 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures — but they come from a cohort whose specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, where a stricture could be called neoplastic on 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, and where all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. Reuse for gate 2 depends entirely on which panel version is run: the 28-gene version used in the original cohort did not detect FGFR2 fusions, which with chromatin-remodelling genes accounts for up to 20% of intrahepatic tumours, while the 161-gene version reports fusions and found actionable alterations in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%). A negative result excludes nothing — negative predictive value in the original cohort was 63%. Downgraded to C for those reasons.

honest.t: Not substituting liver-directed therapy for systemic therapy (gate 5, Avoid).
honest.why: This is the one place the roadmap knowingly disagrees with NCCN, whose wording that arterially directed therapies may be used alone can be read as permitting substitution. The position is supported by AASLD 2023, which states data are insufficient to recommend liver-directed therapy as standard therapy for locally advanced unresectable iCCA, and by the absence of any trial of any catheter or radiation modality against a modern chemo-immunotherapy backbone — none of the HAI, Y90, chemoembolisation, ablation or radiotherapy datasets has such a comparator. It is therefore a position taken in the absence of evidence either way, and it is put to a decision rather than asserted. Alignment worksheet, area 9.

honest.t: Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy after an R1 or node-positive resection.
honest.why: In intrahepatic disease the support is retrospective only. BSG 2023 confines its chemoradiotherapy recommendation after an R1 resection to extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer, and ESMO 2023 states that definitive external beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced cholangiocarcinoma should not be used outside trials. Keeping it as a case-by-case tumour-board discussion rather than a standing rule is the honest position; what is not known is whether it changes anything in iCCA. Alignment worksheet, area 11.

honest.t: Negative adjuvant trials cannot be quoted as evidence that adjuvant therapy is futile.
honest.why: PRODIGE-12 was powered for a hazard ratio of 0.60 on 126 events, its medians fell on a plateau of the curves, and salvage differed sharply by arm (40 of 41 surveillance relapses received gemcitabine-based salvage against 9 of 33 after GEMOX), in a population lower-risk than BILCAP's; it is a failed superiority trial for one regimen. BCAT stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, and its authors calculate only a 2.8% probability of reaching significance even with the planned events — and it excluded intrahepatic disease outright. ASCOT was positive on overall survival but its relapse-free survival endpoint did not reach significance (hazard ratio 0.80, p=0.088) with curves crossing at 6 years, it was analysed at 179 of 285 prespecified events, and S-1 is unavailable outside Asia. Three negative or inapplicable trials do not add up to a demonstration that nothing works, and they do not settle gate 8 either way.

honest.t: Histotripsy for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
honest.why: There is no tumour-specific evidence in this disease at all. The pivotal experience enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and liver metastases, not iCCA, and in its one-year update local control was 63.4% on the primary assessment against 90% post hoc in 47 patients with 52 tumours. FDA device clearance for tumour destruction establishes neither survival benefit nor equivalence to established ablation. Grade D, protocol and registry only, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty.

honest.t: The MMaT-3 exception route, and what it is not.
honest.why: The Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology document is review-board guidance, not OPTN Policy and not a clinical practice guideline; Policy 9.5 defines the standardised exceptions and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is not among them, so every request goes to the review board as a narrative. MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run rather than a fixed national score, an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 under Policy 9.4.E, and extensions generally run in 90-day cycles under 9.4.C. ILTS-ILCA makes no recommendation on allocation priority, exception points or acceptable waitlist dropout, which is what makes the ≤3 cm criterion hard to act on in a system where iCCA earns no priority. Verify the current policy text before any listing decision.

honest.t: A core biopsy before resection of a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass.
honest.why: The sources disagree and the page has chosen a destination-specific rule rather than a universal one. AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation for a definitive iCCA diagnosis, EASL-ILCA recommends biopsy on level 4 evidence with 96% consensus, LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass and recommends it only in unresectable cases, and NCCN states a suspicious mass in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant. ILTS-ILCA makes biopsy mandatory where transplantation is contemplated, to grade differentiation and exclude a mixed tumour. No outcome study compares the two policies in a resectable mass. Alignment worksheet, area 1.

board: Submission: an Epic form captures the clinical question, diagnosis and confirmation status, resectability assessment, molecular status or pending date, liver scores, imaging availability, prior treatment, transplant status, referring clinician and urgency — owner: submitting clinician.

Triage: the coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check completeness, imaging quality, duplicate cases, the urgent lane, and whether the question is actually a decision question — owners: coordinator and chair.
Agenda: stable at least 24 hours ahead, approximately 10–12 decision cases per session, each case carrying one focused question — owner: coordinator.
Urgent lane: a same-week slot with chair approval for time-critical decisions, including biliary obstruction and rapid clinical decline — owner: chair.

Attendance: hepatobiliary and transplant surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, interventional radiology, diagnostic radiology, pathology, hepatology and coordination are all required — owners: specialty leads.
Imaging: adequate and available current imaging, reviewed before the recommendation, not described from a report — owner: diagnostic radiology.
Pathology: pre-alerted for every case requiring confirmation, subtype or molecular status — owner: pathology.
Output: one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered — owner: chair.
Documentation: an Epic note within one business day, in the agreed structured format — owner: named owner.
Registry: the case is closed in the registry with the decision, the modality delivered and the outcome at reassessment — owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships: the referring clinician is informed of the recommendation and who owns the next step. Community-referring relationships are protected explicitly — the pathway returns patients with a plan, it does not capture them — owner: named owner.
dashboard: Proportion of patients profiled before the second-line decision (audit).
Every hepatic arterial infusion case, with toxicity and hepatic progression-free survival (registry).
Liver-directed therapy: modality, stated goal, hepatic progression-free survival and change in liver function (registry).
Adjuvant capecitabine: uptake, completion and recurrence pattern (registry).
Every ablation, with margin and local progression (registry).
Transplant protocol cases — a registry is required if a protocol is opened.
Cases closed in the registry with the decision, the modality delivered and the outcome at reassessment.
Named owner, source edition and date, and update cycle for subsequent NCCN and OPTN checks.

approvals.q: Does the programme run a hepatic arterial infusion service for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?
approvals.why: Supporting data are a single-arm, largely single-institution phase 2 experience. Benefit is plausible and toxicity is real; the deciding variables are pump expertise, nursing infrastructure and case volume.
approvals.audit: Registry: every HAI case, toxicity, hepatic progression-free survival.

approvals.q: Which liver-directed modality is first choice for unresectable liver-confined disease?
approvals.why: No head-to-head comparison exists between HAI, radioembolisation, SBRT and proton therapy.
approvals.audit: Registry: modality, goal, hepatic progression-free survival, liver function change.

approvals.q: Adjuvant capecitabine — offered routinely, or case by case?
approvals.why: BILCAP's primary analysis was not significant; ASCOT's positive result used an agent unavailable here.

approvals.q: Is molecular profiling funded and ordered at diagnosis in practice?
approvals.why: The clinical argument is not in doubt; the obstacle is payer authorisation and ordering discipline.
approvals.audit: Audit: proportion profiled before the second-line decision.

approvals.q: Does the programme open an intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma transplant protocol?
approvals.why: Evidence is retrospective and confined to small tumours first diagnosed on explant pathology, most seen before transplant as presumed hepatocellular carcinoma. Graft stewardship is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question.

approvals.q: What are the thresholds barring each liver-directed modality by liver function?
approvals.why: No comparative data define the cut-offs; they are safety conventions.

approvals.q: Ablation for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma — acceptable, and in whom?
approvals.why: Evidence is substantially weaker than in hepatocellular carcinoma and is retrospective.
approvals.audit: Registry: every ablation, margin, local progression.

approvals.q: Who owns subsequent NCCN and OPTN update checks, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: Source reconciliation is complete in this version. An owner must be assigned to verify subsequent editions and current allocation requirements, ratify the documented institutional positions, and maintain the update cycle.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date plus update cycle.

approvals.q: Is a core biopsy required before resection of a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass, or is destination-specific confirmation enough?
approvals.why: AASLD 2023, BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA require histological confirmation; LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass; NCCN permits treating a suspicious mass in the proper clinical setting as malignant. No outcome study compares the two policies. Alignment worksheet, area 1.
approvals.audit: Audit: proportion of resections performed without pre-operative histology, and the final pathology in each.

approvals.q: Is regional lymphadenectomy mandatory at every iCCA resection, and what minimum node yield is recorded?
approvals.why: LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications; ESMO 2023 recommends routine hepatoduodenal-ligament dissection on level IV evidence; BSG 2023 and AASLD 2023 state neither extent nor yield. The gate 8 adjuvant conversation and the registry both need a nodal denominator. Alignment worksheet, area 5.
approvals.audit: Registry: lymphadenectomy performed, node count, node positivity, and complications attributable to the dissection.

approvals.q: What counts as 'a period of stability' before a transplant referral — what duration, on what therapy, and at what imaging interval?
approvals.why: ILTS-ILCA 2024 attaches no duration to the cirrhotic ≤3 cm recommendation; the six-month figure in our criteria comes from its separate weakly graded non-cirrhotic route and from the Houston Methodist–MD Anderson protocol, whose own authors concede that selecting for stability may be selecting indolent biology. The explant series that supplies our size data required no stability at all.
approvals.audit: Registry: stability interval achieved, regimen, imaging interval, and waitlist dropout for progression.

approvals.q: Does the page name trastuzumab deruxtecan, entrectinib, larotrectinib and selpercatinib, as ESMO 2024 does, or only require that the alterations be captured?
approvals.why: The ESMO recommendations are level III grade A — single-arm or basket-trial evidence — several agents are FDA- but not EMA-approved, and ESMO itself concedes there are no standardised criteria for HER2 assessment in biliary tract cancer. Alignment worksheet, area 14.
approvals.audit: Audit: matched agents prescribed, alteration class, assay used and line of therapy.

approvals.q: Is there a default first-line checkpoint combination, or does the choice stay with the treating oncologist?
approvals.why: No randomised comparison exists between durvalumab and pembrolizumab; ESMO's statement that they are interchangeable is an indirect comparison across trials differing in chemotherapy duration, geography and size. The practical differences are the gemcitabine cycle cap, schedule and access, not efficacy. BSG 2023 also treats oxaliplatin substitution in renal impairment and gemcitabine alone in poor performance status as reasonable, which our page leaves unnamed. Alignment worksheet, area 13.
approvals.audit: Audit: regimen chosen, cycles delivered, any modification and the reason recorded.

approvals.q: Post-resection surveillance — 3-monthly or 6-monthly imaging for the first two years?
approvals.why: NCCN states there are no data supporting a specific surveillance schedule. The argument for 3-monthly is that most recurrences are intrahepatic and some are re-resectable or ablatable; the argument for 6-monthly is that most UK centres practise it and no study shows the shorter interval changes outcome. Alignment worksheet, area 16.
approvals.audit: Audit: interval actually achieved, recurrence pattern, and proportion of recurrences treated with curative intent.

provenance: Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant gate was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability clock in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the ratification item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
